speaker: narrator
context: The Upanishad opens with a story: a father performing a sacrifice gives away everything he owns, while his young son watches.
devanagari:
ॐ उशन् ह वै वाजश्रवसः सर्ववेदसं ददौ ।
तस्य ह नचिकेता नाम पुत्र आस ॥
iast:
oṃ uśan ha vai vājaśravasaḥ sarvavedasaṃ dadau |
tasya ha naciketā nāma putra āsa ||
english: Om. Wanting its reward, the son of Vajashravas, it is told, gave away all he owned. He had a son named Nachiketas.

school_notes.note: The story serves to praise the knowledge that follows. Vājaśravasa performed the Viśvajit sacrifice, in which one gives away everything, wanting its reward.

licence: CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wikisource text); underlying Sanskrit work is public domain

speaker: narrator
context: As the cows are led away as gifts for the priests, faith stirs in the boy Nachiketas.
devanagari:
तँ ह कुमारँ सन्तं दक्षिणासु
नीयमानासु श्रद्धाविवेश सोऽमन्यत ॥
iast:
tam̐ ha kumāram̐ santaṃ dakṣiṇāsu
nīyamānāsu śraddhāviveśa so'manyata ||
english: Though he was only a boy, faith entered him as the gifts were being led away, and he thought:

school_notes.note: Faith, a sense of what is right, prompted by concern for his father's welfare, entered the young boy as the cows were being taken to the priests as their fee.

licence: CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wikisource text); underlying Sanskrit work is public domain

speaker: Nachiketas
context: Nachiketas sees that the cows his father gives away are old and useless, and worries about the result for his father.
devanagari:
पीतोदका जग्धतृणा दुग्धदोहा निरिन्द्रियाः ।
अनन्दा नाम ते लोकास्तान् स गच्छति ता ददत् ॥ ३ ॥
iast:
pītodakā jagdhatṛṇā dugdhadohā nirindriyāḥ |
anandā nāma te lokāstān sa gacchati tā dadat || 3 ||
english: 'They have drunk their water, eaten their grass, given their milk, and are barren. Joyless are the worlds he goes to who gives such cows.'

school_notes.note: The cows given as the fee are old and useless; the sacrificer who gives them goes to the worlds called 'joyless'.

licence: CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wikisource text); underlying Sanskrit work is public domain

speaker: narrator
context: Wanting to save his father's sacrifice, Nachiketas offers himself; his father, angered, says he gives him to Death.
devanagari:
स होवाच पितरं तत कस्मै मां दास्यसीति ।
द्वितीयं तृतीयं तँ होवाच मृत्यवे त्वा ददामीति ॥
iast:
sa hovāca pitaraṃ tata kasmai māṃ dāsyasīti |
dvitīyaṃ tṛtīyaṃ tam̐ hovāca mṛtyave tvā dadāmīti ||
english: He said to his father, 'Father, to whom will you give me?' He said it a second time, and a third. His father said to him, 'To Death I give you!'

school_notes.note: Thinking a son should prevent the bad result of his father's flawed sacrifice, even by giving himself, Nachiketas asked. Ignored, he asked again; his father, angry that this was not how a boy behaves, said, 'I give you to Death.'

licence: CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wikisource text); underlying Sanskrit work is public domain

speaker: Nachiketas
context: Alone, Nachiketas reflects on his father's angry words and wonders what Death could want with him.
devanagari:
बहूनामेमि प्रथमो बहूनामेमि मध्यमः ।
किँ स्विद्यमस्य कर्तव्यं यन्मयाऽद्य करिष्यति ॥
iast:
bahūnāmemi prathamo bahūnāmemi madhyamaḥ |
kim̐ svidyamasya kartavyaṃ yanmayā'dya kariṣyati ||
english: Among many I go as the first; among many I go as one of the middle. What work does Yama have that he will do through me today?

school_notes.note: Among many disciples or sons I rank first or middle, never last; my father spoke in anger, without purpose. Still, so that his word is not false, Nachiketas speaks to his father, who now grieves over what he said.

licence: CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wikisource text); underlying Sanskrit work is public domain

speaker: Nachiketas
context: Nachiketas urges his grieving father to keep his word as good people always have, since mortal life passes like a crop.
devanagari:
अनुपश्य यथा पूर्वे प्रतिपश्य तथाऽपरे ।
सस्यमिव मर्त्यः पच्यते सस्यमिवाजायते पुनः ॥
iast:
anupaśya yathā pūrve pratipaśya tathā'pare |
sasyamiva martyaḥ pacyate sasyamivājāyate punaḥ ||
english: Look back at how those before us acted; look around at how others act now. A mortal ripens like grain, and like grain is born again.

school_notes.note: Consider how your forefathers acted and how good people act now: none made their word false, and no one becomes ageless by breaking it. Mortals ripen and die like grain and are born again, so keep your truth and send me to Yama. The father sent him, and Yama was away for three nights.

licence: CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wikisource text); underlying Sanskrit work is public domain

speaker: Yama's household
context: Nachiketas waits three nights at Death's house; when Yama returns, his household urges him to honour the guest.
devanagari:
वैश्वानरः प्रविशत्यतिथिर्ब्राह्मणो गृहान् ।
तस्यैताँ शान्तिं कुर्वन्ति हर वैवस्वतोदकम् ॥
iast:
vaiśvānaraḥ praviśatyatithirbrāhmaṇo gṛhān |
tasyaitām̐ śāntiṃ kurvanti hara vaivasvatodakam ||
english: A brahmin guest enters houses like fire itself. People make this offering of peace to him: bring water, son of Vivasvat!

school_notes.note: A brahmin guest enters as the fire Vaiśvānara, as if burning; good people calm him with water for the feet and a seat. So bring water, Yama, for neglecting a guest brings harm.

licence: CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wikisource text); underlying Sanskrit work is public domain

speaker: Yama's household
context: Yama's household warns of what is lost when a guest goes unfed.
devanagari:
आशाप्रतीक्षे संगतँ सूनृतां
चेष्टापूर्ते पुत्रपशूँश्च सर्वान् ।
एतद्वृङ्क्ते पुरुषस्याल्पमेधसो
यस्यानश्नन्वसति ब्राह्मणो गृहे ॥
iast:
āśāpratīkṣe saṃgatam̐ sūnṛtāṃ
ceṣṭāpūrte putrapaśūm̐śca sarvān |
etadvṛṅkte puruṣasyālpamedhaso
yasyānaśnanvasati brāhmaṇo gṛhe ||
english: Hopes and expectations, the fruit of good company, kind speech, sacrifices and good works, sons and cattle: all these are taken from the person of little understanding in whose house a brahmin stays without food.

school_notes.note: All these are destroyed for one who lets a brahmin guest stay unfed; so a guest must never be neglected, in any circumstance.

licence: CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wikisource text); underlying Sanskrit work is public domain

speaker: Yama
context: Yama honours Nachiketas, who waited three nights without food, and offers him three boons.
devanagari:
तिस्रो रात्रीर्यदवात्सीर्गृहे मे-
ऽनश्नन् ब्रह्मन्नतिथिर्नमस्यः ।
नमस्तेऽस्तु ब्रह्मन् स्वस्ति मेऽस्तु
तस्मात्प्रति त्रीन्वरान्वृणीष्व ॥
iast:
tisro rātrīryadavātsīrgṛhe me-
'naśnan brahmannatithirnamasyaḥ |
namaste'stu brahman svasti me'stu
tasmātprati trīnvarānvṛṇīṣva ||
english: Brahmin, since you, a guest worthy of honour, have stayed three nights in my house without eating, homage to you, brahmin, and may all go well for me. So choose three boons in return.

school_notes.note: To make amends for the fault of a guest's fasting in his house, and to please Nachiketas further, Yama offers one boon for each night he waited.

licence: CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wikisource text); underlying Sanskrit work is public domain

speaker: Nachiketas
context: For his first boon, Nachiketas asks that his father be at peace, free of anger, and welcome him home.
devanagari:
शान्तसंकल्पः सुमना यथा स्याद्
वीतमन्युर्गौतमो माऽभि मृत्यो ।
त्वत्प्रसृष्टम् माऽभिवदेत्प्रतीत
एतत् त्रयाणां प्रथमं वरं वृणे ॥
iast:
śāntasaṃkalpaḥ sumanā yathā syād
vītamanyurgautamo mā'bhi mṛtyo |
tvatprasṛṣṭam mā'bhivadetpratīta
etat trayāṇāṃ prathamaṃ varaṃ vṛṇe ||
english: That Gautama, my father, may be calm in mind, cheerful, and free of anger towards me, O Death; that he may recognise and greet me when you send me back: this I choose as the first of the three boons.

school_notes.note: That my father stop worrying about what has become of me, be cheerful and free of anger, and recognise me as his son returned: the first boon is my father's contentment.

licence: CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wikisource text); underlying Sanskrit work is public domain

speaker: Yama
context: Yama grants the first boon: the father will welcome his son back, his anger gone.
devanagari:
यथा पुरस्ताद् भविता प्रतीत
औद्दालकिरारुणिर्मत्प्रसृष्टः ।
सुखँ रात्रीः शयिता वीतमन्युः
त्वां ददृशिवान्मृत्युमुखात् प्रमुक्तम् ॥
iast:
yathā purastād bhavitā pratīta
auddālakirāruṇirmatprasṛṣṭaḥ |
sukham̐ rātrīḥ śayitā vītamanyuḥ
tvāṃ dadṛśivānmṛtyumukhāt pramuktam ||
english: Auddalaki Aruni, released by me, will recognise you and be as he was before. Seeing you freed from the jaws of death, he will sleep peacefully at night, his anger gone.

school_notes.note: Your father will be as affectionate towards you as before; with my permission he will sleep happily, free of anger, having seen you freed from death.

licence: CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wikisource text); underlying Sanskrit work is public domain

speaker: Nachiketas
context: Nachiketas describes the heaven-world, free of fear, age and sorrow, before asking his second boon.
devanagari:
स्वर्गे लोके न भयं किंचनास्ति
न तत्र त्वं न जरया बिभेति ।
उभे तीर्त्वाऽशनायापिपासे
शोकातिगो मोदते स्वर्गलोके ॥
iast:
svarge loke na bhayaṃ kiṃcanāsti
na tatra tvaṃ na jarayā bibheti |
ubhe tīrtvā'śanāyāpipāse
śokātigo modate svargaloke ||
english: In the heaven-world there is no fear at all; you are not there, and no one fears old age. Having crossed beyond both hunger and thirst, free of sorrow, one rejoices in the heaven-world.

school_notes.note: In heaven there is no fear from disease or the like, and Death does not strike suddenly as here; beyond hunger, thirst and sorrow, one rejoices.

licence: CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wikisource text); underlying Sanskrit work is public domain

speaker: Nachiketas
context: For his second boon, Nachiketas asks Death to teach him the sacred fire that leads to heaven.
devanagari:
स त्वमग्निँ स्वर्ग्यमध्येषि मृत्यो
प्रब्रूहि त्वँ श्रद्दधानाय मह्यम् ।
स्वर्गलोका अमृतत्वं भजन्त
एतद् द्वितीयेन वृणे वरेण ॥
iast:
sa tvamagnim̐ svargyamadhyeṣi mṛtyo
prabrūhi tvam̐ śraddadhānāya mahyam |
svargalokā amṛtatvaṃ bhajanta
etad dvitīyena vṛṇe vareṇa ||
english: You know, Death, the fire that leads to heaven; explain it to me, for I have faith. Those who reach heaven gain immortality. This I choose as my second boon.

school_notes.note: Those who build this fire reach heaven and gain 'immortality', meaning the state of the gods; Nachiketas asks for knowledge of the fire as his second boon.

licence: CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wikisource text); underlying Sanskrit work is public domain

speaker: Yama
context: Death agrees to teach the fire that leads to heaven.
devanagari:
प्र ते ब्रवीमि तदु मे निबोध
स्वर्ग्यमग्निं नचिकेतः प्रजानन् ।
अनन्तलोकाप्तिमथो प्रतिष्ठां
विद्धि त्वमेतं निहितं गुहायाम् ॥
iast:
pra te bravīmi tadu me nibodha
svargyamagniṃ naciketaḥ prajānan |
anantalokāptimatho pratiṣṭhāṃ
viddhi tvametaṃ nihitaṃ guhāyām ||
english: I will explain it to you; learn it from me, Nachiketas, for I know the fire that leads to heaven. Know this fire, the way to the endless world and its foundation, as hidden in the secret place.

school_notes.note: The fire is the means to heaven and also the support of the world as Virāj; 'hidden in the secret place' means set in the intellect of the wise.

licence: CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wikisource text); underlying Sanskrit work is public domain

speaker: narrator
context: The Upanishad reports that Death taught the fire ritual in detail and Nachiketas repeated it back correctly.
devanagari:
लोकादिमग्निं तमुवाच तस्मै
या इष्टका यावतीर्वा यथा वा ।
स चापि तत्प्रत्यवदद्यथोक्तं
अथास्य मृत्युः पुनरेवाह तुष्टः ॥
iast:
lokādimagniṃ tamuvāca tasmai
yā iṣṭakā yāvatīrvā yathā vā |
sa cāpi tatpratyavadadyathoktaṃ
athāsya mṛtyuḥ punarevāha tuṣṭaḥ ||
english: He told him of that fire, the beginning of the worlds: what bricks, how many, and how they are laid. And Nachiketas repeated it back just as it was told. Then Death, pleased, spoke again.

school_notes.note: These are the Upanishad's own words. Death taught the fire, the first embodied being, with the bricks, their number and arrangement; pleased with the repetition, he wished to give a boon beyond the three.

licence: CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wikisource text); underlying Sanskrit work is public domain

speaker: Yama
context: Pleased with his student, Death gives Nachiketas an extra boon: the fire will bear his name.
devanagari:
तमब्रवीत् प्रीयमाणो महात्मा
वरं तवेहाद्य ददामि भूयः ।
तवैव नाम्ना भविताऽयमग्निः
सृङ्कां चेमामनेकरूपां गृहाण ॥
iast:
tamabravīt prīyamāṇo mahātmā
varaṃ tavehādya dadāmi bhūyaḥ |
tavaiva nāmnā bhavitā'yamagniḥ
sṛṅkāṃ cemāmanekarūpāṃ gṛhāṇa ||
english: The great-souled one, delighted, said to him: 'I give you another boon here and now: this fire shall be known by your name. And take this many-coloured chain.'

school_notes.note: Seeing the student's fitness, Death gives a fourth boon: the fire named after Nachiketas, and a precious, many-coloured necklace; or, alternatively, the path of ritual action with its many results.

licence: CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wikisource text); underlying Sanskrit work is public domain

speaker: Yama
context: Death praises the fire ritual and the peace it brings to one who performs it fully.
devanagari:
त्रिणाचिकेतस्त्रिभिरेत्य सन्धिं
त्रिकर्मकृत्तरति जन्ममृत्यू ।
ब्रह्मजज्ञं देवमीड्यं विदित्वा
निचाय्येमाँ शान्तिमत्यन्तमेति ॥
iast:
triṇāciketastribhiretya sandhiṃ
trikarmakṛttarati janmamṛtyū |
brahmajajñaṃ devamīḍyaṃ viditvā
nicāyyemām̐ śāntimatyantameti ||
english: One who has kindled the Nachiketa fire three times, joined with the three, doing the three works, crosses over birth and death. Knowing the god born of Brahman, all-knowing and worthy of praise, and realising him, one reaches this peace for ever.

school_notes.note: 'The three' are mother, father and teacher, or alternatively scripture, tradition and the virtuous; 'the three works' are sacrifice, study and giving. Knowing Virāj, born of Hiraṇyagarbha, one reaches the state of Virāj by combining ritual and meditation.

licence: CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wikisource text); underlying Sanskrit work is public domain

speaker: Yama
context: Death concludes his praise of the fire ritual and its reward in heaven.
devanagari:
त्रिणाचिकेतस्त्रयमेतद्विदित्वा
य एवं विद्वाँश्चिनुते नाचिकेतम् ।
स मृत्युपाशान् पुरतः प्रणोद्य
शोकातिगो मोदते स्वर्गलोके ॥
iast:
triṇāciketastrayametadviditvā
ya evaṃ vidvām̐ścinute nāciketam |
sa mṛtyupāśān purataḥ praṇodya
śokātigo modate svargaloke ||
english: One who knows these three and, knowing this, builds the Nachiketa fire, casts off the nooses of death beforehand and, beyond sorrow, rejoices in the heaven-world.

school_notes.note: The 'nooses of death' are wrongdoing, ignorance, passion and hatred; such a person casts them off even before the body falls and rejoices in the world of Virāj.

licence: CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wikisource text); underlying Sanskrit work is public domain

speaker: Yama
context: Death closes the second boon and invites Nachiketas to choose his third.
devanagari:
एष तेऽग्निर्नचिकेतः स्वर्ग्यो
यमवृणीथा द्वितीयेन वरेण ।
एतमग्निं तवैव प्रवक्ष्यन्ति जनासः
तृतीयं वरं नचिकेतो वृणीष्व ॥
iast:
eṣa te'gnirnaciketaḥ svargyo
yamavṛṇīthā dvitīyena vareṇa |
etamagniṃ tavaiva pravakṣyanti janāsaḥ
tṛtīyaṃ varaṃ naciketo vṛṇīṣva ||
english: This is your fire that leads to heaven, Nachiketas, which you chose with your second boon. People will call this fire by your name. Choose your third boon, Nachiketas.

school_notes.note: Until the third boon is given, Death remains in debt. What has been taught so far concerns ritual; what follows teaches knowledge of the Self, which alone removes the ignorance at the root of rebirth, and the coming temptations test Nachiketas's detachment.

licence: CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wikisource text); underlying Sanskrit work is public domain

speaker: Nachiketas
context: For his third boon, Nachiketas asks the great question: does a person still exist after death?
devanagari:
येयं प्रेते विचिकित्सा मनुष्ये-
ऽस्तीत्येके नायमस्तीति चैके ।
एतद्विद्यामनुशिष्टस्त्वयाऽहं
वराणामेष वरस्तृतीयः ॥
iast:
yeyaṃ prete vicikitsā manuṣye-
'stītyeke nāyamastīti caike |
etadvidyāmanuśiṣṭastvayā'haṃ
varāṇāmeṣa varastṛtīyaḥ ||
english: There is this doubt about a person who has died: some say 'he is', others say 'he is not'. Taught by you, I would know this. This is the third of my boons.

school_notes.note: Some say there is a Self, distinct from body, senses, mind and intellect, that goes on to another body; others deny it. Neither perception nor inference settles the question, and the highest human good depends on knowing the answer.

licence: CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wikisource text); underlying Sanskrit work is public domain

speaker: Yama
context: To test Nachiketas, Death says the question is too subtle and asks him to choose another boon.
devanagari:
देवैरत्रापि विचिकित्सितं पुरा
न हि सुविज्ञेयमणुरेष धर्मः ।
अन्यं वरं नचिकेतो वृणीष्व
मा मोपरोत्सीरति मा सृजैनम् ॥
iast:
devairatrāpi vicikitsitaṃ purā
na hi suvijñeyamaṇureṣa dharmaḥ |
anyaṃ varaṃ naciketo vṛṇīṣva
mā moparotsīrati mā sṛjainam ||
english: Even the gods of old had doubts about this; it is not easy to understand, this subtle matter. Choose another boon, Nachiketas. Do not press me; release me from this one.

school_notes.note: To test whether Nachiketas is fit for self-knowledge, Death says the Self is subtle and hard to know even when heard; 'do not press me' as a creditor presses a debtor.

licence: CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wikisource text); underlying Sanskrit work is public domain

speaker: Nachiketas
context: Nachiketas refuses to give up his question: no teacher equals Death, and no boon equals this one.
devanagari:
देवैरत्रापि विचिकित्सितं किल
त्वं च मृत्यो यन्न सुज्ञेयमात्थ ।
वक्ता चास्य त्वादृगन्यो न लभ्यो
नान्यो वरस्तुल्य एतस्य कश्चित् ॥
iast:
devairatrāpi vicikitsitaṃ kila
tvaṃ ca mṛtyo yanna sujñeyamāttha |
vaktā cāsya tvādṛganyo na labhyo
nānyo varastulya etasya kaścit ||
english: Even the gods had doubts about this, you say, Death, and it is not easy to understand; yet no other teacher like you can be found, and no other boon equals this one.

school_notes.note: Since even the wise find it hard, no teacher equal to you can be found; this boon leads to the highest good, so no other boon, all of which bring impermanent results, can equal it.

licence: CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wikisource text); underlying Sanskrit work is public domain

speaker: Yama
context: Death tries to tempt Nachiketas away from his question with descendants, wealth, land and long life (1.1.23-1.1.25).
devanagari:
शतायुषः पुत्रपौत्रान्वृणीष्वा
बहून्पशून् हस्तिहिरण्यमश्वान् ।
भूमेर्महदायतनं वृणीष्व
स्वयं च जीव शरदो यावदिच्छसि ॥
iast:
śatāyuṣaḥ putrapautrānvṛṇīṣvā
bahūnpaśūn hastihiraṇyamaśvān |
bhūmermahadāyatanaṃ vṛṇīṣva
svayaṃ ca jīva śarado yāvadicchasi ||
english: Choose sons and grandsons who will live a hundred years, many cattle, elephants, gold and horses. Choose a great expanse of land, and live yourself as many autumns as you wish.

school_notes.note: Death offers long-lived descendants, cattle, elephants, gold, horses and a kingdom, and, since all these would be useless with a short life, as long a life as Nachiketas wants.

licence: CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wikisource text); underlying Sanskrit work is public domain

speaker: Yama
context: Death continues to tempt Nachiketas with wealth, long life, kingship and every pleasure.
devanagari:
एतत्तुल्यं यदि मन्यसे वरं
वृणीष्व वित्तं चिरजीविकां च ।
महाभूमौ नचिकेतस्त्वमेधि
कामानां त्वा कामभाजं करोमि ॥
iast:
etattulyaṃ yadi manyase varaṃ
vṛṇīṣva vittaṃ cirajīvikāṃ ca |
mahābhūmau naciketastvamedhi
kāmānāṃ tvā kāmabhājaṃ karomi ||
english: If you think of any boon equal to this, choose it: wealth and long life. Be a ruler on the wide earth, Nachiketas. I will make you one who enjoys all desires.

school_notes.note: Choose wealth with long life, be king of a great land; Death, a god whose will comes true, offers to make Nachiketas enjoy all desires, divine and human.

licence: CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wikisource text); underlying Sanskrit work is public domain

speaker: Yama
context: Death's final temptation offers heavenly women and every rare pleasure, if only Nachiketas will stop asking about death.
devanagari:
ये ये कामा दुर्लभा मर्त्यलोके
सर्वान् कामाँश्छन्दतः प्रार्थयस्व ।
इमा रामाः सरथाः सतूर्या
न हीदृशा लम्भनीया मनुष्यैः ।
आभिर्मत्प्रत्ताभिः परिचारयस्व
नचिकेतो मरणं माऽनुप्राक्षीः ॥
iast:
ye ye kāmā durlabhā martyaloke
sarvān kāmām̐śchandataḥ prārthayasva |
imā rāmāḥ sarathāḥ satūryā
na hīdṛśā lambhanīyā manuṣyaiḥ |
ābhirmatprattābhiḥ paricārayasva
naciketo maraṇaṃ mā'nuprākṣīḥ ||
english: Whatever desires are hard to win in the world of mortals, ask for them all as you wish: these lovely women with chariots and music, such as no mortal can obtain. Be served by them, my gift to you. Nachiketas, do not ask about death.

school_notes.note: The women are heavenly nymphs, who cannot be won without the favour of gods like Death. 'Do not ask about death' means: do not ask whether one exists after death, a question as pointless as examining a crow's teeth.

licence: CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wikisource text); underlying Sanskrit work is public domain

speaker: Nachiketas
context: Unmoved, Nachiketas replies that all these pleasures are fleeting and wear out the senses.
devanagari:
श्वोभावा मर्त्यस्य यदन्तकैतत्
सर्वेंद्रियाणां जरयंति तेजः ।
अपि सर्वं जीवितमल्पमेव
तवैव वाहास्तव नृत्यगीते ॥
iast:
śvobhāvā martyasya yadantakaitat
sarveṃdriyāṇāṃ jarayaṃti tejaḥ |
api sarvaṃ jīvitamalpameva
tavaiva vāhāstava nṛtyagīte ||
english: These last only till tomorrow, Death, and they wear away the vigour of all a mortal's senses. Even a whole life is short. Keep your chariots; keep your dance and song.

school_notes.note: The pleasures offered may not last even until tomorrow, and they drain the senses' vigour along with merit, wisdom and fame. Even the life of Brahmā is short, let alone ours.

licence: CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wikisource text); underlying Sanskrit work is public domain

speaker: Nachiketas
context: Nachiketas says wealth never satisfies anyone, and he wants only the answer to his question.
devanagari:
न वित्तेन तर्पणीयो मनुष्यो
लप्स्यामहे वित्तमद्राक्ष्म चेत्त्वा ।
जीविष्यामो यावदीशिष्यसि त्वं
वरस्तु मे वरणीयः स एव ॥
iast:
na vittena tarpaṇīyo manuṣyo
lapsyāmahe vittamadrākṣma cettvā |
jīviṣyāmo yāvadīśiṣyasi tvaṃ
varastu me varaṇīyaḥ sa eva ||
english: No one is satisfied by wealth. We shall have wealth if we have seen you; we shall live as long as you rule. But the boon I would choose is that one alone.

school_notes.note: No one in the world is ever seen to be satisfied by gaining wealth. Having met Death, wealth and life will come anyway; the only boon worth choosing is knowledge of the Self.

licence: CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wikisource text); underlying Sanskrit work is public domain

speaker: Nachiketas
context: Nachiketas asks who, having glimpsed the immortal, would still want a long life of fading pleasures.
devanagari:
अजीर्यताममृतानामुपेत्य
जीर्यन्मर्त्यः क्वधःस्थः प्रजानन् ।
अभिध्यायन् वर्णरतिप्रमोदान्
अतिदीर्घे जीविते को रमेत ॥
iast:
ajīryatāmamṛtānāmupetya
jīryanmartyaḥ kvadhaḥsthaḥ prajānan |
abhidhyāyan varṇaratipramodān
atidīrghe jīvite ko rameta ||
english: Having come near the ageless and immortal, what ageing mortal here below, who understands, would delight in a very long life, dwelling on the pleasures of beauty and love?

school_notes.note: Who, knowing there is something higher to be gained from the immortals, would choose unstable things like sons and gold? Reflecting on how fleeting beauty and pleasure are, what discerning person would delight in a long life?

licence: CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wikisource text); underlying Sanskrit work is public domain

speaker: Nachiketas
context: Nachiketas holds to his question about what lies beyond death and chooses no other boon.
devanagari:
यस्मिन्निदं विचिकित्सन्ति मृत्यो
यत्साम्पराये महति ब्रूहि नस्तत् ।
योऽयं वरो गूढमनुप्रविष्टो
नान्यं तस्मान्नचिकेता वृणीते ॥
iast:
yasminnidaṃ vicikitsanti mṛtyo
yatsāmparāye mahati brūhi nastat |
yo'yaṃ varo gūḍhamanupraviṣṭo
nānyaṃ tasmānnaciketā vṛṇīte ||
english: That about which people doubt, Death, concerning the great passing beyond: tell us that. This boon, which enters into what is hidden: Nachiketas chooses no other.

school_notes.note: Tell us the certain knowledge of the Self concerning the next world. The closing words are the Upanishad's own: Nachiketas does not choose, even in thought, any boon of impermanent things.

licence: CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wikisource text); underlying Sanskrit work is public domain

speaker: Yama
context: Satisfied that Nachiketas is ready, Death begins his teaching by contrasting the good with the merely pleasant.
devanagari:
अन्यच्छ्रेयोऽन्यदुतैव प्रेय-
स्ते उभे नानार्थे पुरुषँ सिनीतः ।
तयोः श्रेय आददानस्य साधु
भवति हीयतेऽर्थाद्य उ प्रेयो वृणीते ॥
iast:
anyacchreyo'nyadutaiva preya-
ste ubhe nānārthe puruṣam̐ sinītaḥ |
tayoḥ śreya ādadānasya sādhu
bhavati hīyate'rthādya u preyo vṛṇīte ||
english: The good is one thing, the pleasant quite another. Both, with different aims, bind a person. All goes well for the one who takes the good; whoever chooses the pleasant falls short of the goal.

school_notes.note: Everyone pursues one or the other, prosperity or liberation, and one person cannot follow both, since they are as opposed as knowledge and ignorance. Whoever takes the good alone fares well; the short-sighted who choose the pleasant lose the lasting goal.

licence: CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wikisource text); underlying Sanskrit work is public domain

speaker: Yama
context: Death says the wise tell the good from the pleasant and choose the good, while the foolish choose comfort.
devanagari:
श्रेयश्च प्रेयश्च मनुष्यमेतः
तौ सम्परीत्य विविनक्ति धीरः ।
श्रेयो हि धीरोऽभि प्रेयसो वृणीते
प्रेयो मन्दो योगक्षेमाद्वृणीते ॥
iast:
śreyaśca preyaśca manuṣyametaḥ
tau samparītya vivinakti dhīraḥ |
śreyo hi dhīro'bhi preyaso vṛṇīte
preyo mando yogakṣemādvṛṇīte ||
english: The good and the pleasant both come to a person. The wise one examines them closely and tells them apart. The wise choose the good over the pleasant; the foolish choose the pleasant, for getting and keeping.

school_notes.note: Like a swan separating milk from water, the wise weigh the two and choose the good. The dull, unable to discern, choose the pleasant, such as cattle and sons, for the growth and protection of the body.

licence: CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wikisource text); underlying Sanskrit work is public domain

speaker: Yama
context: Death praises Nachiketas for rejecting the pleasures offered and not taking the path of wealth where many sink.
devanagari:
स त्वं प्रियान्प्रियरूपांश्च कामान्
अभिध्यायन्नचिकेतोऽत्यस्राक्षीः ।
नैतां सृङ्कां वित्तमयीमवाप्तो
यस्यां मज्जन्ति बहवो मनुष्याः ॥
iast:
sa tvaṃ priyānpriyarūpāṃśca kāmān
abhidhyāyannaciketo'tyasrākṣīḥ |
naitāṃ sṛṅkāṃ vittamayīmavāpto
yasyāṃ majjanti bahavo manuṣyāḥ ||
english: But you, Nachiketas, having reflected on desires dear and lovely to look at, have let them go. You have not taken this chain of wealth in which many people sink.

school_notes.note: Tempted again and again, you weighed sons and nymphs as impermanent and worthless and gave them up; how wise you are. You did not take the despised path of wealth, on which fools sink.

licence: CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wikisource text); underlying Sanskrit work is public domain

speaker: Yama
context: Death says knowledge and ignorance lead in opposite directions, and Nachiketas has shown himself a seeker of knowledge.
devanagari:
दूरमेते विपरीते विषूची
अविद्या या च विद्येति ज्ञाता ।
विद्याभीप्सिनं नचिकेतसं मन्ये
न त्वा कामा बहवोऽलोलुपन्त ॥
iast:
dūramete viparīte viṣūcī
avidyā yā ca vidyeti jñātā |
vidyābhīpsinaṃ naciketasaṃ manye
na tvā kāmā bahavo'lolupanta ||
english: Far apart and leading different ways are these two: ignorance and what is known as knowledge. I consider Nachiketas a seeker of knowledge, for many desires did not distract you.

school_notes.note: Like darkness and light, ignorance and knowledge lead to rebirth and to liberation. Since the many pleasures did not pull you from the path of the good, I count you a seeker of knowledge.

licence: CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wikisource text); underlying Sanskrit work is public domain

speaker: Yama
context: Death describes people who think themselves wise while living in ignorance: the blind led by the blind.
devanagari:
अविद्यायामन्तरे वर्तमानाः
स्वयं धीराः पण्डितंमन्यमानाः ।
दन्द्रम्यमाणाः परियन्ति मूढा
अन्धेनैव नीयमाना यथान्धाः ॥
iast:
avidyāyāmantare vartamānāḥ
svayaṃ dhīrāḥ paṇḍitaṃmanyamānāḥ |
dandramyamāṇāḥ pariyanti mūḍhā
andhenaiva nīyamānā yathāndhāḥ ||
english: Living in the midst of ignorance, thinking themselves wise and learned, the deluded go round and round, staggering, like the blind led by the blind.

school_notes.note: Caught in ignorance as in thick darkness, bound by a hundred ropes of craving for sons and cattle, yet thinking themselves wise and learned, the deluded wander through old age, death and disease, like the blind led by the blind on a rough road.

licence: CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wikisource text); underlying Sanskrit work is public domain

speaker: Yama
context: Death says those absorbed in wealth and this world alone come under his power again and again.
devanagari:
न साम्परायः प्रतिभाति बालं
प्रमाद्यन्तं वित्तमोहेन मूढम् ।
अयं लोको नास्ति पर इति मानी
पुनः पुनर्वशमापद्यते मे ॥
iast:
na sāmparāyaḥ pratibhāti bālaṃ
pramādyantaṃ vittamohena mūḍham |
ayaṃ loko nāsti para iti mānī
punaḥ punarvaśamāpadyate me ||
english: The passage beyond does not shine for the childish, careless and deluded by wealth. 'This world exists, there is no other,' thinks such a person, and falls into my power again and again.

school_notes.note: The means to the next world does not occur to the immature, absorbed in sons and cattle and blinded by wealth. Thinking only this visible world of women, food and drink exists, they are born and die again and again; most people are like this.

licence: CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wikisource text); underlying Sanskrit work is public domain

speaker: Yama
context: Death says the Self is rarely heard of, rarely understood, and rarely taught well.
devanagari:
श्रवणायापि बहुभिर्यो न लभ्यः
शृण्वन्तोऽपि बहवो यं न विद्युः ।
आश्चर्यो वक्ता कुशलोऽस्य लब्धा
आश्चर्यो ज्ञाता कुशलानुशिष्टः ॥
iast:
śravaṇāyāpi bahubhiryo na labhyaḥ
śṛṇvanto'pi bahavo yaṃ na vidyuḥ |
āścaryo vaktā kuśalo'sya labdhā
āścaryo jñātā kuśalānuśiṣṭaḥ ||
english: Many do not even get to hear of it; many who hear of it do not understand it. Wonderful is the one who teaches it, skilled the one who gains it; wonderful the one who knows it, taught by the skilled.

school_notes.note: Few even hear of the Self, and of those who hear, few understand. A teacher of it is rare among many, and rare is the one who comes to know it when taught by a skilled teacher.

licence: CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wikisource text); underlying Sanskrit work is public domain

speaker: Yama
context: Death says the Self cannot be understood when taught by an ordinary person, but only by one who has realised it.
devanagari:
न नरेणावरेण प्रोक्त एष
सुविज्ञेयो बहुधा चिन्त्यमानः ।
अनन्यप्रोक्ते गतिरत्र नास्ति
अणीयान् ह्यतर्क्यमणुप्रमाणात् ॥
iast:
na nareṇāvareṇa prokta eṣa
suvijñeyo bahudhā cintyamānaḥ |
ananyaprokte gatiratra nāsti
aṇīyān hyatarkyamaṇupramāṇāt ||
english: Taught by an inferior person, it is not easily understood, though thought about in many ways. When it is taught by one who is not separate from it, no uncertainty remains, for it is finer than the finest and beyond argument.

school_notes.note: Argued about in many ways, as existing or not, as doer or not, the Self cannot be well understood from an ordinary teacher. Taught by a teacher who sees no separation, being one with Brahman, no speculation about it remains; he also offers the readings 'nothing further remains to be known' and 'no failure to understand remains'.

licence: CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wikisource text); underlying Sanskrit work is public domain

speaker: Yama
context: Death says this understanding comes through teaching, not argument, and praises Nachiketas's steadfastness.
devanagari:
नैषा तर्केण मतिरापनेया
प्रोक्तान्येनैव सुज्ञानाय प्रेष्ठ ।
यां त्वमापः सत्यधृतिर्बतासि
त्वादृङ्नो भूयान्नचिकेतः प्रष्टा ॥
iast:
naiṣā tarkeṇa matirāpaneyā
proktānyenaiva sujñānāya preṣṭha |
yāṃ tvamāpaḥ satyadhṛtirbatāsi
tvādṛṅno bhūyānnaciketaḥ praṣṭā ||
english: This understanding is not reached by reasoning, dearest; taught by another, it is easily understood. You have gained it, for your resolve is true. May we find a questioner like you, Nachiketas!

school_notes.note: This insight from scripture is not won, and should not be given up, through mere argument, since a reasoner without scripture says whatever he imagines. Taught by a teacher versed in scripture, it becomes clear; Death praises Nachiketas to commend the teaching to come.

licence: CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wikisource text); underlying Sanskrit work is public domain

speaker: Yama
context: Death admits that impermanent means cannot reach the eternal; his own position was gained through ritual.
devanagari:
जानाम्यहं शेवधिरित्यनित्यं
न ह्यध्रुवैः प्राप्यते हि ध्रुवं तत् ।
ततो मया नाचिकेतश्चितोऽग्निः
अनित्यैर्द्रव्यैः प्राप्तवानस्मि नित्यम् ॥
iast:
jānāmyahaṃ śevadhirityanityaṃ
na hyadhruvaiḥ prāpyate hi dhruvaṃ tat |
tato mayā nāciketaścito'gniḥ
anityairdravyaiḥ prāptavānasmi nityam ||
english: I know that what is called treasure is impermanent, for the permanent is not reached by impermanent things. So I built the Nachiketa fire with impermanent things, and gained what is lasting.

school_notes.note: The 'treasure' of ritual results is impermanent, and the eternal Self cannot be reached by impermanent means. Knowing this, Death still built the fire with things like cattle, and so gained his own place, which is 'lasting' only relatively.

licence: CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wikisource text); underlying Sanskrit work is public domain

speaker: Yama
context: Death praises Nachiketas for seeing every worldly reward and letting all of them go.
devanagari:
कामस्याप्तिं जगतः प्रतिष्ठां
क्रतोरानन्त्यमभयस्य पारम् ।
स्तोममहदुरुगायं प्रतिष्ठां दृष्ट्वा
धृत्या धीरो नचिकेतोऽत्यस्राक्षीः ॥
iast:
kāmasyāptiṃ jagataḥ pratiṣṭhāṃ
kratorānantyamabhayasya pāram |
stomamahadurugāyaṃ pratiṣṭhāṃ dṛṣṭvā
dhṛtyā dhīro naciketo'tyasrākṣīḥ ||
english: You saw the fulfilment of desire, the foundation of the world, the endless fruit of ritual, the far shore of fearlessness, the great and praised wide path, the firm standing; and, wise and steadfast, Nachiketas, you let them all go.

school_notes.note: You saw all the fruits that culminate in the state of Hiraṇyagarbha, where every desire is fulfilled, the support of the world, with its powers, and yet, wanting only the highest, you let go of all worldly enjoyment with firmness. How excellent you are.

licence: CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wikisource text); underlying Sanskrit work is public domain

speaker: Yama
context: Death says that the wise, realising the hidden Self through inward meditation, leave both joy and sorrow behind.
devanagari:
तं दुर्दर्शं गूढमनुप्रविष्टं
गुहाहितं गह्वरेष्ठं पुराणम् ।
अध्यात्मयोगाधिगमेन देवं
मत्वा धीरो हर्षशोकौ जहाति ॥
iast:
taṃ durdarśaṃ gūḍhamanupraviṣṭaṃ
guhāhitaṃ gahvareṣṭhaṃ purāṇam |
adhyātmayogādhigamena devaṃ
matvā dhīro harṣaśokau jahāti ||
english: That god, hard to see, hidden deep, set in the secret place, dwelling in the depths, ancient: realising him through the yoga of the inner self, the wise leave joy and sorrow behind.

school_notes.note: The Self is hard to see because it is subtle and hidden by knowledge of sense objects; it is found in the intellect. The 'yoga of the inner self' is withdrawing the mind from objects and fixing it on the Self; knowing it, the wise drop joy and sorrow, since the Self neither gains nor loses.

licence: CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wikisource text); underlying Sanskrit work is public domain

speaker: Yama
context: Death tells Nachiketas that whoever grasps the subtle Self finds true joy, and that the way is open for him.
devanagari:
एतच्छ्रुत्वा सम्परिगृह्य मर्त्यः
प्रवृह्य धर्म्यमणुमेतमाप्य ।
स मोदते मोदनीयँ हि लब्ध्वा
विवृतँ सद्म नचिकेतसं मन्ये ॥
iast:
etacchrutvā samparigṛhya martyaḥ
pravṛhya dharmyamaṇumetamāpya |
sa modate modanīyam̐ hi labdhvā
vivṛtam̐ sadma naciketasaṃ manye ||
english: A mortal who has heard this, grasped it fully, drawn out this subtle Self that is true to dharma, and reached it, rejoices, having found what is truly worth rejoicing in. I think the house stands open for Nachiketas.

school_notes.note: Having heard it from the teacher and separated the subtle Self from the body, the wise rejoice in it. The house of Brahman stands open to you: Death considers Nachiketas fit for liberation.

licence: CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wikisource text); underlying Sanskrit work is public domain

speaker: Nachiketas
context: Nachiketas asks Death to describe what lies beyond right and wrong, cause and effect, past and future.
devanagari:
अन्यत्र धर्मादन्यत्राधर्मा-
दन्यत्रास्मात्कृताकृतात् ।
अन्यत्र भूताच्च भव्याच्च
यत्तत्पश्यसि तद्वद ॥
iast:
anyatra dharmādanyatrādharmā-
danyatrāsmātkṛtākṛtāt |
anyatra bhūtācca bhavyācca
yattatpaśyasi tadvada ||
english: Tell me what you see as other than dharma and other than adharma, other than what is done and not done, other than what has been and what is to be.

school_notes.note: He asks for what is beyond scriptural duty, its fruits and its agents, beyond wrongdoing, beyond effect and cause, and not limited by past, future or present: whatever lies beyond all ordinary dealings.

licence: CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wikisource text); underlying Sanskrit work is public domain

speaker: Yama
context: Death names the goal that all the Vedas point to: the syllable Om.
devanagari:
सर्वे वेदा यत्पदमामनन्ति
तपाँसि सर्वाणि च यद्वदन्ति ।
यदिच्छन्तो ब्रह्मचर्यं चरन्ति
तत्ते पदँ संग्रहेण ब्रवीम्योमित्येतत् ॥
iast:
sarve vedā yatpadamāmananti
tapām̐si sarvāṇi ca yadvadanti |
yadicchanto brahmacaryaṃ caranti
tatte padam̐ saṃgraheṇa bravīmyomityetat ||
english: The goal that all the Vedas declare, that all austerities speak of, desiring which people live as celibate students: that goal I tell you briefly. It is Om.

school_notes.note: The goal all the Vedas teach and all austerities aim at, for which people live at their teacher's house, is what the word Om names and also what Om stands for as a symbol.

licence: CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wikisource text); underlying Sanskrit work is public domain

speaker: Yama
context: Death says the syllable Om is Brahman itself, and knowing it brings whatever one seeks.
devanagari:
एतद्ध्येवाक्षरं ब्रह्म एतद्ध्येवाक्षरं परम् ।
एतद्ध्येवाक्षरं ज्ञात्वा यो यदिच्छति तस्य तत् ॥
iast:
etaddhyevākṣaraṃ brahma etaddhyevākṣaraṃ param |
etaddhyevākṣaraṃ jñātvā yo yadicchati tasya tat ||
english: This syllable is Brahman; this syllable is the highest. Knowing this syllable, whatever one wants becomes one's own.

school_notes.note: Om is the symbol of both the lower and the higher Brahman. Worshipping it as Brahman, one gains whichever one seeks: the higher is to be known, the lower to be reached.

licence: CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wikisource text); underlying Sanskrit work is public domain

speaker: Yama
context: Death calls Om the best support for reaching Brahman.
devanagari:
एतदालम्बनँ श्रेष्ठमेतदालम्बनं परम् ।
एतदालम्बनं ज्ञात्वा ब्रह्मलोके महीयते ॥
iast:
etadālambanam̐ śreṣṭhametadālambanaṃ param |
etadālambanaṃ jñātvā brahmaloke mahīyate ||
english: This support is the best; this support is the highest. Knowing this support, one is honoured in the world of Brahman.

school_notes.note: Of all supports for reaching Brahman, Om is the best. Om has been given as a symbol for those of slow or middling understanding; next the Upanishad describes the Self directly.

licence: CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wikisource text); underlying Sanskrit work is public domain

speaker: Yama
context: Death describes the Self directly: never born, never dying, untouched when the body is killed (compare Gita 2.20).
devanagari:
न जायते म्रियते वा विपश्चिन्
नायं कुतश्चिन्न बभूव कश्चित् ।
अजो नित्यः शाश्वतोऽयं पुराणो
न हन्यते हन्यमाने शरीरे ॥
iast:
na jāyate mriyate vā vipaścin
nāyaṃ kutaścinna babhūva kaścit |
ajo nityaḥ śāśvato'yaṃ purāṇo
na hanyate hanyamāne śarīre ||
english: The wise one is not born and does not die. It did not come from anywhere, and nothing came from it. Unborn, eternal, everlasting, ancient, it is not killed when the body is killed.

school_notes.note: Birth and death, the first and last of all changes, are denied of the Self, and with them every change. It has no cause and produces nothing other than itself; it does not decline and does not grow, being 'ancient' yet always new. So it is not harmed when weapons strike the body, any more than space is.

licence: CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wikisource text); underlying Sanskrit work is public domain

speaker: Yama
context: Death says the one who thinks he kills and the one who thinks he is killed both misunderstand the Self (compare Gita 2.19).
devanagari:
हन्ता चेन्मन्यते हन्तुँ हतश्चेन्मन्यते हतम् ।
उभौ तौ न विजानीतो नायँ हन्ति न हन्यते ॥
iast:
hantā cenmanyate hantum̐ hataścenmanyate hatam |
ubhau tau na vijānīto nāyam̐ hanti na hanyate ||
english: If the killer thinks he kills, and if the one killed thinks he is killed, neither of them understands: this does not kill, and is not killed.

school_notes.note: Whoever takes the body for the Self and thinks 'I will kill him' or 'I am killed' does not know the Self, which, unchanging like space, neither kills nor is killed. So the round of merit and demerit belongs only to those who do not know the Self, not to the knower of Brahman.

licence: CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wikisource text); underlying Sanskrit work is public domain

speaker: Yama
context: Death says the Self, smaller than the smallest and greater than the greatest, is seen by one free of desire.
devanagari:
अणोरणीयान्महतो महीया-
नात्माऽस्य जन्तोर्निहितो गुहायाम् ।
तमक्रतुः पश्यति वीतशोको
धातुप्रसादान्महिमानमात्मनः ॥
iast:
aṇoraṇīyānmahato mahīyā-
nātmā'sya jantornihito guhāyām |
tamakratuḥ paśyati vītaśoko
dhātuprasādānmahimānamātmanaḥ ||
english: Smaller than the small, greater than the great, the Self is set in the heart of every creature. One free of desire sees it, and is free of sorrow: through the clarity of the faculties, one sees the greatness of the Self.

school_notes.note: Whatever is small or great exists only through the Self, so the Self is smaller than the smallest and greater than the greatest. One without desire, whose mind has turned from all objects, finds the faculties grow clear, sees the Self's greatness, untouched by growth or decline, as 'I am this', and is free of grief.

licence: CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wikisource text); underlying Sanskrit work is public domain

speaker: Yama
context: Death describes the Self in paradoxes and says few can know it.
devanagari:
आसीनो दूरं व्रजति शयानो याति सर्वतः ।
कस्तं मदामदं देवं मदन्यो ज्ञातुमर्हति ॥
iast:
āsīno dūraṃ vrajati śayāno yāti sarvataḥ |
kastaṃ madāmadaṃ devaṃ madanyo jñātumarhati ||
english: Sitting still, it travels far; lying down, it goes everywhere. Who but me can know that god, who rejoices and does not rejoice?

school_notes.note: The Self seems to have contradictory qualities, moving and unmoving, joyful and not, through its limiting conditions, so it is hard to know except for the subtle-minded. In sleep, when the senses rest, it seems to go everywhere; in waking, it seems to travel far with the mind.

licence: CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wikisource text); underlying Sanskrit work is public domain

speaker: Yama
context: Death says the wise, knowing the bodiless, all-pervading Self within changing bodies, do not grieve.
devanagari:
अशरीरँ शरीरेष्वनवस्थेष्ववस्थितम् ।
महान्तं विभुमात्मानं मत्वा धीरो न शोचति ॥
iast:
aśarīram̐ śarīreṣvanavastheṣvavasthitam |
mahāntaṃ vibhumātmānaṃ matvā dhīro na śocati ||
english: Bodiless within bodies, steady among the unsteady, great and all-pervading: knowing the Self this way, the wise do not grieve.

school_notes.note: The Self is bodiless like space, yet dwells unchanging in the bodies of gods, ancestors and humans, which never stay the same. Knowing it as 'I am this', the wise have no ground for grief.

licence: CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wikisource text); underlying Sanskrit work is public domain

speaker: Yama
context: Death says the Self is not won by learning or cleverness, but reveals itself to the one it chooses.
devanagari:
नायमात्मा प्रवचनेन लभ्यो
न मेधया न बहुना श्रुतेन ।
यमेवैष वृणुते तेन लभ्यः
तस्यैष आत्मा विवृणुते तनूँ स्वाम् ॥
iast:
nāyamātmā pravacanena labhyo
na medhayā na bahunā śrutena |
yamevaiṣa vṛṇute tena labhyaḥ
tasyaiṣa ātmā vivṛṇute tanūm̐ svām ||
english: This Self is not won by teaching, nor by intellect, nor by much learning. It is won only by the one whom it chooses; to that one the Self reveals its own form.

school_notes.note: Not by mastering many Vedas, nor by the power to retain texts, nor by much hearing alone. He reads the choosing the other way round: the Self is won by the one who chooses the Self alone, so it is won through the Self, and to one who desires only the Self, it reveals its true nature.

licence: CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wikisource text); underlying Sanskrit work is public domain

speaker: Yama
context: Death names the conditions for knowing the Self: turning from wrongdoing and having a calm, collected mind.
devanagari:
नाविरतो दुश्चरितान्नाशान्तो नासमाहितः ।
नाशान्तमानसो वाऽपि प्रज्ञानेनैनमाप्नुयात् ॥
iast:
nāvirato duścaritānnāśānto nāsamāhitaḥ |
nāśāntamānaso vā'pi prajñānenainamāpnuyāt ||
english: One who has not turned away from wrongdoing, who is not calm, not collected, whose mind is not at peace, cannot reach it through knowledge.

school_notes.note: One who has not stopped forbidden acts, whose senses are restless, whose mind is scattered, or who is collected but still anxious for the fruit of concentration, does not reach the Self. One who has turned from wrongdoing and sense-craving, is collected and at peace, and has a teacher, does.

licence: CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wikisource text); underlying Sanskrit work is public domain

speaker: Yama
context: Death ends the section with an image: the Self consumes even the highest powers, so how can an unprepared person know it?
devanagari:
यस्य ब्रह्म च क्षत्रं च उभे भवत ओदनः ।
मृत्युर्यस्योपसेचनं क इत्था वेद यत्र सः ॥
iast:
yasya brahma ca kṣatraṃ ca ubhe bhavata odanaḥ |
mṛtyuryasyopasecanaṃ ka itthā veda yatra saḥ ||
english: For whom priesthood and kingship are both just rice, and death is the sauce poured on it: who, like this, knows where it is?

school_notes.note: The Self consumes even the brahmin and the kshatriya, upholders and protectors of dharma, as food, with death, which takes everything, as a mere sauce. How could an ordinary person, lacking the means just described, know where that Self is?

licence: CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wikisource text); underlying Sanskrit work is public domain

speaker: Yama
context: Death begins a new section with an image of two selves in the heart, as different as shadow and sunlight.
devanagari:
ऋतं पिबन्तौ सुकृतस्य लोके
गुहां प्रविष्टौ परमे परार्धे ।
छायातपौ ब्रह्मविदो वदन्ति
पञ्चाग्नयो ये च त्रिणाचिकेताः ॥
iast:
ṛtaṃ pibantau sukṛtasya loke
guhāṃ praviṣṭau parame parārdhe |
chāyātapau brahmavido vadanti
pañcāgnayo ye ca triṇāciketāḥ ||
english: Two drink the truth of their deeds in the world of good works, having entered the secret place, the highest seat. Knowers of Brahman call them shadow and light, as do householders who keep the five fires and those who have thrice kindled the Nachiketa fire.

school_notes.note: Only one, the individual self, experiences the fruits of action; the other is said to 'drink' only by association. Both dwell in the cave of the intellect in the heart, yet differ like shadow and sunlight, one bound in worldly life, the other free; not only renunciants but householders say so.

licence: CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wikisource text); underlying Sanskrit work is public domain

speaker: Yama
context: Death prays to master both the ritual fire and the imperishable Brahman beyond fear.
devanagari:
यः सेतुरीजानानामक्षरं ब्रह्म यत् परम् ।
अभयं तितीर्षतां पारं [https://puranastudy.000space.com/pur_index15/nachiketa.htm नाचिकेतँ] शकेमहि ॥
iast:
yaḥ seturījānānāmakṣaraṃ brahma yat param |
abhayaṃ titīrṣatāṃ pāraṃ [https://puranastudy.000space.com/pur_index15/nachiketa.htm nāciketam̐] śakemahi ||
english: May we be able to master the Nachiketa fire, the bridge for those who sacrifice, and the imperishable, highest Brahman, the fearless far shore for those who wish to cross over.

school_notes.note: The Nachiketa fire is a bridge across suffering for ritualists; the imperishable Brahman is the fearless shore beyond worldly life for those who seek to cross. Both, the lower and the higher Brahman, are to be known.

licence: CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wikisource text); underlying Sanskrit work is public domain

speaker: Yama
context: Death gives the image of the chariot: the Self rides in the body, with the intellect as driver and the mind as reins (1.3.3-1.3.9).
devanagari:
आत्मानँ रथिनं विद्धि शरीरँ रथमेव तु ।
बुद्धिं तु सारथिं विद्धि मनः प्रग्रहमेव च ॥
iast:
ātmānam̐ rathinaṃ viddhi śarīram̐ rathameva tu |
buddhiṃ tu sārathiṃ viddhi manaḥ pragrahameva ca ||
english: Know the Self as the rider in the chariot, the body as the chariot, the intellect as the charioteer, and the mind as the reins.

school_notes.note: The individual self is the owner of the chariot; the body is the chariot, pulled by the senses; the deciding intellect is the driver, since most bodily action is directed by it; the mind, which forms intentions, is the reins by which the senses are guided.

licence: CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wikisource text); underlying Sanskrit work is public domain

speaker: Yama
context: Death continues the chariot image: the senses are horses and their objects the roads.
devanagari:
इन्द्रियाणि हयानाहुर्विषयाँ स्तेषु गोचरान् ।
आत्मेन्द्रियमनोयुक्तं भोक्तेत्याहुर्मनीषिणः ॥
iast:
indriyāṇi hayānāhurviṣayām̐ steṣu gocarān |
ātmendriyamanoyuktaṃ bhoktetyāhurmanīṣiṇaḥ ||
english: The senses, they say, are the horses, and the objects of sense are the roads they run on. The Self joined with body, senses and mind is the one who experiences, so the wise say.

school_notes.note: The Self alone does not experience anything; being an experiencer comes from its limiting conditions, the intellect and the rest. Only on this understanding can the 'highest place of Viṣṇu' later be recognised as one's own Self.

licence: CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wikisource text); underlying Sanskrit work is public domain

speaker: Yama
context: Death says a person without understanding and an undisciplined mind has senses like wild horses.
devanagari:
यस्त्वविज्ञानवान्भवत्ययुक्तेन मनसा सदा ।
तस्येन्द्रियाण्यवश्यानि दुष्टाश्वा इव सारथेः ॥
iast:
yastvavijñānavānbhavatyayuktena manasā sadā |
tasyendriyāṇyavaśyāni duṣṭāśvā iva sāratheḥ ||
english: Whoever lacks understanding, with a mind never held steady, has senses out of control, like a charioteer's unruly horses.

school_notes.note: When the intellect, the driver, lacks skill and discernment and the mind, the reins, is never held firm, the senses cannot be checked, like untrained horses under a poor driver.

licence: CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wikisource text); underlying Sanskrit work is public domain

speaker: Yama
context: Death says a person with understanding and a steady mind has senses like well-trained horses.
devanagari:
यस्तु विज्ञानवान्भवति युक्तेन मनसा सदा ।
तस्येन्द्रियाणि वश्यानि सदश्वा इव सारथेः ॥
iast:
yastu vijñānavānbhavati yuktena manasā sadā |
tasyendriyāṇi vaśyāni sadaśvā iva sāratheḥ ||
english: But whoever has understanding, with a mind always held steady, has senses under control, like a charioteer's good horses.

school_notes.note: A skilled driver with a steady mind can urge on or hold back the senses at will, like a good driver with well-trained horses.

licence: CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wikisource text); underlying Sanskrit work is public domain

speaker: Yama
context: Death says one without understanding or self-control does not reach the goal but stays in the cycle of birth and death.
devanagari:
यस्त्वविज्ञानवान्भवत्यमनस्कः सदाऽशुचिः ।
न स तत्पदमाप्नोति संसारं चाधिगच्छति ॥
iast:
yastvavijñānavānbhavatyamanaskaḥ sadā'śuciḥ |
na sa tatpadamāpnoti saṃsāraṃ cādhigacchati ||
english: Whoever lacks understanding, is unmindful and always impure, does not reach that goal, but goes on into the round of rebirth.

school_notes.note: With such a driver the rider does not reach the imperishable goal; not only does he miss liberation, he goes on through birth and death.

licence: CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wikisource text); underlying Sanskrit work is public domain

speaker: Yama
context: Death says one with understanding and self-control reaches the goal from which there is no return.
devanagari:
यस्तु विज्ञानवान्भवति समनस्कः सदा शुचिः ।
स तु तत्पदमाप्नोति यस्माद्भूयो न जायते ॥
iast:
yastu vijñānavānbhavati samanaskaḥ sadā śuciḥ |
sa tu tatpadamāpnoti yasmādbhūyo na jāyate ||
english: But whoever has understanding, is mindful and always pure, reaches that goal from which one is not born again.

school_notes.note: The rider with a discerning driver and a steady mind is always pure, reaches the goal, and, never slipping from it, is not born again into worldly life.

licence: CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wikisource text); underlying Sanskrit work is public domain

speaker: Yama
context: Death completes the chariot image: with understanding as driver and the mind as reins, one reaches the highest place.
devanagari:
विज्ञानसारथिर्यस्तु मनः प्रग्रहवान्नरः ।
सोऽध्वनः पारमाप्नोति तद्विष्णोः परमं पदम् ॥
iast:
vijñānasārathiryastu manaḥ pragrahavānnaraḥ |
so'dhvanaḥ pāramāpnoti tadviṣṇoḥ paramaṃ padam ||
english: The person whose charioteer is understanding, who holds the reins of the mind, reaches the end of the road: that highest place of Vishnu.

school_notes.note: Such a person reaches the end of the journey of worldly life and is freed from all bonds. 'Viṣṇu' is the all-pervading Brahman, the supreme Self called Vāsudeva; its highest place is its true nature, to be reached by moving inward from the gross to the subtle.

licence: CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wikisource text); underlying Sanskrit work is public domain

speaker: Yama
context: Death lays out a ladder inward: beyond the senses are their objects, then mind, intellect and the great self.
devanagari:
इन्द्रियेभ्यः परा ह्यर्था अर्थेभ्यश्च परं मनः ।
मनसस्तु परा बुद्धिर्बुद्धेरात्मा महान्परः ॥
iast:
indriyebhyaḥ parā hyarthā arthebhyaśca paraṃ manaḥ |
manasastu parā buddhirbuddherātmā mahānparaḥ ||
english: Beyond the senses are their objects; beyond the objects is the mind; beyond the mind is the intellect; beyond the intellect is the great self.

school_notes.note: Each is subtler, greater and more inward than the one before. The 'great self' is the first-born Hiraṇyagarbha, born from the unmanifest, the inner self of all beings' intellects.

licence: CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wikisource text); underlying Sanskrit work is public domain

speaker: Yama
context: Death completes the ladder: beyond the great self is the unmanifest, and beyond that the Person, the highest goal.
devanagari:
महतः परमव्यक्तमव्यक्तात्पुरुषः परः ।
पुरुषान्न परं किंचित्सा [https://sa.wikisource.org/s/3gst काष्ठा] सा परा गतिः ॥
iast:
mahataḥ paramavyaktamavyaktātpuruṣaḥ paraḥ |
puruṣānna paraṃ kiṃcitsā [https://sa.wikisource.org/s/3gst kāṣṭhā] sā parā gatiḥ ||
english: Beyond the great is the unmanifest; beyond the unmanifest is the Person. Beyond the Person there is nothing: that is the end, that is the highest goal.

school_notes.note: The unmanifest is the seed of the whole world, resting in the supreme Self as a banyan rests in its seed. Beyond it is the Person, pure consciousness, beyond which there is nothing; reaching it is called 'going' only figuratively, since it is one's own inner Self.

licence: CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wikisource text); underlying Sanskrit work is public domain

speaker: Yama
context: Death says the Self is hidden in all beings but can be seen by a focused, subtle mind.
devanagari:
एष सर्वेषु भूतेषु गूढोऽऽत्मा न प्रकाशते ।
दृश्यते त्वग्र्यया बुद्ध्या सूक्ष्मया सूक्ष्मदर्शिभिः ॥
iast:
eṣa sarveṣu bhūteṣu gūḍho''tmā na prakāśate |
dṛśyate tvagryayā buddhyā sūkṣmayā sūkṣmadarśibhiḥ ||
english: This Self, hidden in all beings, does not shine forth; but it is seen by those of subtle sight, with a sharp and subtle intellect.

school_notes.note: The Self is hidden by ignorance and māyā: people are told 'you are the supreme Self' and do not accept it, yet take the body to be themselves without being told (compare Gita 7.25). It is seen by a refined, one-pointed intellect that has learned to see ever subtler things.

licence: CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wikisource text); underlying Sanskrit work is public domain

speaker: Yama
context: Death gives a method of meditation: draw speech into mind, mind into intellect, and so on into the peaceful Self.
devanagari:
यच्छेद्वाङ्मनसी प्राज्ञस्तद्यच्छेज्ज्ञान आत्मनि ।
ज्ञानमात्मनि महति नियच्छेत्तद्यच्छेच्छान्त आत्मनि ॥
iast:
yacchedvāṅmanasī prājñastadyacchejjñāna ātmani |
jñānamātmani mahati niyacchettadyacchecchānta ātmani ||
english: The wise should draw speech into the mind, the mind into the knowing self, the knowing self into the great self, and that into the peaceful Self.

school_notes.note: 'Speech' stands for all the senses. Withdraw them into the mind, the mind into the intellect, the intellect into the first-born great self, and that into the peaceful, unchanging Self, the witness of all; then, as a mirage vanishes when seen for what it is, one rests in oneself, at peace.

licence: CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wikisource text); underlying Sanskrit work is public domain

speaker: Yama
context: Death's call to action: wake up, seek out the wise and learn, for the path is as narrow as a razor's edge.
devanagari:
उत्तिष्ठत जाग्रत
प्राप्य वरान्निबोधत ।
क्षुरस्य धारा निशिता दुरत्यया
दुर्गं पथस्तत्कवयो वदन्ति ॥

uttiṣṭhata jāgrata
prāpya varānnibodhata |
kṣurasya dhārā niśitā duratyayā
durgaṃ pathastatkavayo vadanti ||
english: Arise! Awake! Find the great ones and learn. Sharp as a razor's edge and hard to cross: so the wise describe this path.

school_notes.note: Rise from the sleep of beginningless ignorance; go to excellent teachers who know the Self and understand 'I am that'. Scripture says this with a mother's compassion. The path is hard to tread, like a razor's edge, because what is to be known is so subtle.

speaker: Yama
context: Death describes Brahman as beyond all the senses and without beginning or end; realising it frees one from death.
devanagari:
अशब्दमस्पर्शमरूपमव्ययं
तथाऽरसं नित्यमगन्धवच्च यत् ।
अनाद्यनन्तं महतः परं ध्रुवं
निचाय्य तन्मृत्युमुखात् प्रमुच्यते ॥
iast:
aśabdamasparśamarūpamavyayaṃ
tathā'rasaṃ nityamagandhavacca yat |
anādyanantaṃ mahataḥ paraṃ dhruvaṃ
nicāyya tanmṛtyumukhāt pramucyate ||
english: Without sound, touch, form, taste or smell, imperishable, eternal, without beginning or end, beyond the great, unchanging: realising that, one is freed from the jaws of death.

school_notes.note: What has sound and the other qualities decays; Brahman, lacking them, does not, and so is eternal; having no cause and no effect into which it dissolves, it has neither beginning nor end. Realising it, one is freed from death, meaning ignorance, desire and action.

speaker: Upanishad
context: The Upanishad praises the telling and hearing of Nachiketas's story.
devanagari:
नाचिकेतमुपाख्यानं मृत्युप्रोक्तँ सनातनम् ।
उक्त्वा श्रुत्वा च मेधावी ब्रह्मलोके महीयते ॥

nāciketamupākhyānaṃ mṛtyuproktam̐ sanātanam |

english: Having told and heard this ancient story of Nachiketas, told by Death, the wise are honoured in the world of Brahman.

school_notes.note: The story of the three vallīs, received by Nachiketas and taught by Death, is ancient because it is Vedic; whoever tells it to brahmins or hears it from teachers is honoured in Brahman, the world that is Brahman.

speaker: Upanishad
context: The first chapter closes by praising the recitation of this teaching.

य इमं परमं गुह्यं श्रावयेद् ब्रह्मसंसदि ।
प्रयतः श्राद्धकाले वा तदानन्त्याय कल्पते ।
तदानन्त्याय कल्पत इति ॥

ya imaṃ paramaṃ guhyaṃ śrāvayed brahmasaṃsadi |
prayataḥ śrāddhakāle vā tadānantyāya kalpate |

english: Whoever, purified, recites this supreme secret in an assembly of brahmins or at the time of the rites for the dead, gains what is endless; gains what is endless.

school_notes.note: Whoever recites the text and its meaning before an assembly of brahmins, or to those eating at a memorial rite, makes that rite yield endless fruit. The repetition marks the end of the chapter.

speaker: Yama
context: Opening the second chapter, Death says the senses are made to look outward, and only a rare person turns within.
devanagari:
पराञ्चि खानि व्यतृणत् स्वयम्भू-
स्तस्मात्पराङ्पश्यति नान्तरात्मन् ।
कश्चिद्धीरः प्रत्यगात्मानमैक्ष-
दावृत्तचक्षुरमृतत्वमिच्छन् ॥
iast:
parāñci khāni vyatṛṇat svayambhū-
stasmātparāṅpaśyati nāntarātman |
kaściddhīraḥ pratyagātmānamaikṣa-
dāvṛttacakṣuramṛtatvamicchan ||
english: The Self-existent pierced the openings of the senses outward, so one looks outward, not within. A certain wise one, seeking immortality, turned his eyes inward and saw the Self within.

school_notes.note: The Lord made the senses face outward to sound and the other objects, so people perceive what is not the Self. Rarely, like turning back against a river's current, a discerning person withdraws the senses and sees the inner Self.

speaker: Yama
context: Death contrasts the childish, who chase outward pleasures into death's net, with the wise, who seek nothing unstable.
devanagari:
पराचः कामाननुयन्ति बाला-
स्ते मृत्योर्यन्ति विततस्य पाशम् ।
अथ धीरा अमृतत्वं विदित्वा
ध्रुवमध्रुवेष्विह न प्रार्थयन्ते ॥
iast:
parācaḥ kāmānanuyanti bālā-
ste mṛtyoryanti vitatasya pāśam |
atha dhīrā amṛtatvaṃ viditvā
dhruvamadhruveṣviha na prārthayante ||
english: The childish run after outward pleasures and walk into the wide-spread net of death. But the wise, knowing what is truly immortal, seek nothing here among the unstable things.

school_notes.note: Those who chase external desires fall into the net of repeated birth, death, old age and disease. The wise, knowing the unshakeable immortality of resting in the Self, seek nothing among impermanent things and rise above the desires for sons, wealth and worlds.

licence: CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wikisource text); underlying Sanskrit work is public domain

speaker: Yama
context: Death says the Self is that by which we know every sense experience; nothing is beyond it.
devanagari:
येन रूपं रसं गन्धं शब्दान् स्पर्शाँश्च मैथुनान् ।
एतेनैव विजानाति किमत्र परिशिष्यते ।
एतद्वै तत् ॥
iast:
yena rūpaṃ rasaṃ gandhaṃ śabdān sparśām̐śca maithunān |
etenaiva vijānāti kimatra pariśiṣyate |
etadvai tat ||
english: That by which one knows form, taste, smell, sounds, touches and the pleasures of love: by this alone one knows. What remains here? This, truly, is that.

school_notes.note: People think the body knows, but the body is itself made of form and the rest and is known like them. Everything is known by the Self, distinct from the body, as iron burns by the fire in it; nothing remains unknown to it, so it is all-knowing. 'This is that' which Nachiketas asked about.

licence: CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wikisource text); underlying Sanskrit work is public domain

speaker: Yama
context: Death says the wise, knowing the Self that witnesses both dreaming and waking, do not grieve.
devanagari:
स्वप्नान्तं जागरितान्तं चोभौ येनानुपश्यति ।
महान्तं विभुमात्मानं मत्वा धीरो न शोचति ॥

svapnāntaṃ jāgaritāntaṃ cobhau yenānupaśyati |
mahāntaṃ vibhumātmānaṃ matvā dhīro na śocati ||
english: That by which one perceives both dreaming and waking: knowing it as the great, all-pervading Self, the wise do not grieve.

school_notes.note: The Self by which people perceive what appears in dream and in waking: realising it directly as 'I am the supreme Self', the wise do not grieve.

licence: CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wikisource text); underlying Sanskrit work is public domain

speaker: Yama
context: Death says one who knows the Self as close at hand and lord of past and future no longer needs to guard himself.
devanagari:
य इमं मध्वदं वेद आत्मानं जीवमन्तिकात् ।
ईशानं भूतभव्यस्य न ततो विजुगुप्सते ।
एतद्वै तत् ॥
iast:
ya imaṃ madhvadaṃ veda ātmānaṃ jīvamantikāt |
īśānaṃ bhūtabhavyasya na tato vijugupsate |
etadvai tat ||
english: Whoever knows this Self, the one who tastes the honey, the living one, close at hand, lord of past and future, no longer seeks to shield himself. This, truly, is that.

school_notes.note: As long as one stands amid fear and thinks oneself impermanent, one wants to protect oneself; once one knows the Self as eternal and non-dual, who would guard what, and against whom?

licence: CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wikisource text); underlying Sanskrit work is public domain

speaker: Yama
context: Death identifies the first-born of creation, dwelling in the heart, with Brahman.
devanagari:
यः पूर्वं तपसो जातमद्भ्यः पूर्वमजायत ।
गुहां प्रविश्य तिष्ठन्तं यो भूतेभिर्व्यपश्यत ।

yaḥ pūrvaṃ tapaso jātamadbhyaḥ pūrvamajāyata |
guhāṃ praviśya tiṣṭhantaṃ yo bhūtebhirvyapaśyata |
etadvai tat ||
english: The one born first from austerity, born before the waters, who entered the secret place and dwells there with the elements: whoever sees him sees this. This, truly, is that.

school_notes.note: The first-born is Hiraṇyagarbha, born from Brahman's knowledge before the five elements. Whoever sees him dwelling in the heart of every being, with body and senses, sees Brahman itself.

speaker: Yama
context: Death identifies Aditi, made of all the gods and dwelling in the heart, with Brahman.
devanagari:
या प्राणेन संभवत्यदितिर्देवतामयी ।
गुहां प्रविश्य तिष्ठन्तीं या भूतेभिर्व्यजायत ।
एतद्वै तत् ॥

yā prāṇena saṃbhavatyaditirdevatāmayī |
guhāṃ praviśya tiṣṭhantīṃ yā bhūtebhirvyajāyata |
etadvai tat ||
english: Aditi, made of all the gods, who comes forth with the breath of life, who entered the secret place and dwells there, who was born with the elements: this, truly, is that.

school_notes.note: Aditi, so called because she 'eats' sound and the other objects, embodies all the deities and arises from Brahman as life-breath, that is, as Hiraṇyagarbha; she too dwells in the heart.

licence: CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wikisource text); underlying Sanskrit work is public domain

speaker: Yama
context: Death identifies Agni, the sacred fire hidden in the fire-sticks and worshipped daily, with Brahman.

अरण्योर्निहितो जातवेदा गर्भ इव सुभृतो गर्भिणीभिः ।
दिवे दिवे ईड्यो जागृवद्भिर्हविष्मद्भिर्मनुष्येभिरग्निः ।

araṇyornihito jātavedā garbha iva subhṛto garbhiṇībhiḥ |
dive dive īḍyo jāgṛvadbhirhaviṣmadbhirmanuṣyebhiragniḥ |
etadvai tat ||
english: Agni, the knower of all, hidden in the two fire-sticks like an unborn child well cared for by expectant mothers, is to be praised day after day by watchful people bringing offerings. This, truly, is that.

school_notes.note: Agni is hidden in the fire-sticks of the ritual and, for yogis, in the heart; ritualists and meditators, vigilant and bringing offerings or meditation, praise him daily. That too is Brahman.

licence: CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wikisource text); underlying Sanskrit work is public domain

speaker: Yama
context: Death says that from which the sun rises and into which it sets is Brahman, beyond which nothing goes.
devanagari:
यतश्चोदेति सूर्योऽस्तं यत्र च गच्छति ।
तं देवाः सर्वेऽर्पितास्तदु नात्येति कश्चन ।
एतद्वै तत् ॥
iast:
yataścodeti sūryo'staṃ yatra ca gacchati |
taṃ devāḥ sarve'rpitāstadu nātyeti kaścana |
etadvai tat ||
english: That from which the sun rises and into which it sets; in it all the gods are fixed, and no one ever goes beyond it. This, truly, is that.

school_notes.note: The sun rises from and sets into prāṇa, in which all the gods, outer and inner, are fixed like spokes in a hub; that too is Brahman, and nothing passes beyond being it.

licence: CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wikisource text); underlying Sanskrit work is public domain

speaker: Yama
context: Death warns that whoever sees separateness in the one reality goes from death to death.
devanagari:
यदेवेह तदमुत्र यदमुत्र तदन्विह ।
मृत्योः स मृत्युमाप्नोति य इह नानेव पश्यति ॥
iast:
yadeveha tadamutra yadamutra tadanviha |
mṛtyoḥ sa mṛtyumāpnoti ya iha nāneva paśyati ||
english: What is here is there; what is there is here. Whoever sees difference here goes from death to death.

school_notes.note: What appears here with body and senses is the same as the pure Brahman 'there', and vice versa. One deluded into thinking 'I am other than Brahman' goes through death after death; so one should see 'I am Brahman, full like space'.

licence: CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wikisource text); underlying Sanskrit work is public domain

speaker: Yama
context: Death repeats that the oneness of reality is grasped by the mind, and seeing difference leads from death to death.
devanagari:
मनसैवेदमाप्तव्यं नेह नानाऽस्ति किंचन ।
मृत्योः स मृत्युं गच्छति य इह नानेव पश्यति ॥
iast:
manasaivedamāptavyaṃ neha nānā'sti kiṃcana |
mṛtyoḥ sa mṛtyuṃ gacchati ya iha nāneva paśyati ||
english: By the mind alone is this to be reached: there is no difference here at all. Whoever sees difference here goes from death to death.

school_notes.note: Brahman, of one nature, is to be reached by a mind refined by teacher and scripture as 'the Self alone exists'. Once reached, the ignorance that shows diversity is gone; whoever still imposes even the slightest difference goes from death to death.

licence: CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wikisource text); underlying Sanskrit work is public domain

speaker: Yama
context: Death describes the Self dwelling in the heart, the size of a thumb, lord of past and future.
devanagari:
अङ्गुष्ठमात्रः पुरुषो मध्य आत्मनि तिष्ठति ।
ईशानं भूतभव्यस्य न ततो विजुगुप्सते ।
एतद्वै तत् ॥

aṅguṣṭhamātraḥ puruṣo madhya ātmani tiṣṭhati |
īśānaṃ bhūtabhavyasya na tato vijugupsate |
etadvai tat ||
english: A person the size of a thumb dwells in the middle of the body, lord of past and future. Knowing him, one no longer seeks to shield oneself. This, truly, is that.

school_notes.note: 'The size of a thumb' refers to the space of the heart, which is about that size; the Person who fills everything seems so through the mind dwelling there, as space seems the size of the hollow in a bamboo joint. Knowing him, one has no more fear, as before.

licence: CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wikisource text); underlying Sanskrit work is public domain

speaker: Yama
context: Death says the Self in the heart is like a smokeless flame, the same today and tomorrow.
devanagari:
अङ्गुष्ठमात्रः पुरुषो ज्योतिरिवाधूमकः ।
ईशानो भूतभव्यस्य स एवाद्य स उ श्वः ।
एतद्वै तत् ॥

aṅguṣṭhamātraḥ puruṣo jyotirivādhūmakaḥ |
īśāno bhūtabhavyasya sa evādya sa u śvaḥ |
etadvai tat ||
english: The person the size of a thumb is like a flame without smoke, lord of past and future. He is the same today, and he will be tomorrow. This, truly, is that.

school_notes.note: He is eternal and unchanging, present in beings today and tomorrow alike, with none like him born again. This answers the view 'he does not exist' raised in Nachiketas's question, and also refutes the doctrine that everything lasts only a moment.

licence: CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wikisource text); underlying Sanskrit work is public domain

speaker: Yama
context: Death gives an image of seeing things as separate: like rain scattering down a mountain.
devanagari:
यथोदकं दुर्गे वृष्टं पर्वतेषु विधावति ।
एवं धर्मान् पृथक् पश्यंस्तानेवानुविधावति ॥

yathodakaṃ durge vṛṣṭaṃ parvateṣu vidhāvati |
evaṃ dharmān pṛthak paśyaṃstānevānuvidhāvati ||
english: As rain falling on high ground runs off in all directions down the hills, so one who sees things as separate runs after them.

school_notes.note: As rain on a high place scatters and is lost in the valleys, one who sees selves as different in each body follows those differences, taking body after body.

licence: CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wikisource text); underlying Sanskrit work is public domain

speaker: Yama
context: Death gives the opposite image: the knower's self becomes one with reality, like pure water poured into pure water.
devanagari:
यथोदकं शुद्धे शुद्धमासिक्तं तादृगेव भवति ।
एवं मुनेर्विजानत आत्मा भवति गौतम ॥

yathodakaṃ śuddhe śuddhamāsiktaṃ tādṛgeva bhavati |
evaṃ munervijānata ātmā bhavati gautama ||
english: As pure water poured into pure water becomes just like it, so, Gautama, becomes the self of the sage who knows.

school_notes.note: So the Self becomes one for the knowing sage. Therefore one should give up the divisive views of bad logicians and nihilists and, with pride subdued, honour the vision of oneness taught by the Veda, which cares for us more than a thousand mothers and fathers.

licence: CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wikisource text); underlying Sanskrit work is public domain

speaker: Yama
context: Death compares the body to a city with eleven gates whose ruler is the unborn Self; meditating on him ends grief.

अनुष्ठाय न शोचति विमुक्तश्च विमुच्यते ।
एतद्वै तत् ॥

puramekādaśadvāramajasyāvakracetasaḥ |
anuṣṭhāya na śocati vimuktaśca vimucyate |

english: There is a city with eleven gates belonging to the unborn one whose awareness is never crooked. Meditating on him, one grieves no more, and, freed, is set free. This, truly, is that.

school_notes.note: The body is a city with eleven openings, seven in the head, the navel, two below and one at the crown, serving a ruler distinct from it. Its lord is the unborn, unchanging Self; meditating on him with right knowledge, free of all desires, one has no occasion for grief or fear.

speaker: Yama
context: Death names the one Self in many forms: sun, air, fire, guest, and all that is born.

हँसः शुचिषद्वसुरान्तरिक्षसद्-

नृषद्वरसदृतसद्व्योमसद्
अब्जा गोजा ऋतजा अद्रिजा ऋतं बृहत् ॥

Though it is all things, it is truth and great, being the cause of all.

speaker: Yama
context: Death says the Self moves the breath and all the senses serve it, like subjects serving a king.
devanagari:
ऊर्ध्वं प्राणमुन्नयत्यपानं प्रत्यगस्यति ।
मध्ये वामनमासीनं विश्वे देवा उपासते ॥

ūrdhvaṃ prāṇamunnayatyapānaṃ pratyagasyati |

english: He leads the in-breath upward and drives the out-breath down. All the gods serve that dwarf seated in the middle.

speaker: Yama
context: Death asks what remains in the body when the embodied Self leaves it, pointing to the Self as distinct.
devanagari:
अस्य विस्रंसमानस्य शरीरस्थस्य देहिनः ।
देहाद्विमुच्यमानस्य किमत्र परिशिष्यते ।

asya visraṃsamānasya śarīrasthasya dehinaḥ |
dehādvimucyamānasya kimatra pariśiṣyate |
etadvai tat ||
english: When this embodied one, dwelling in the body, slips away and is freed from the body, what remains here? This, truly, is that.

school_notes.note: When the Self departs, the whole complex of body and senses loses its power and falls apart at once, like a city whose lord has fled; so the Self is something other than them.

licence: CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wikisource text); underlying Sanskrit work is public domain

speaker: Yama
context: Death says people live not by their breath but by something else on which the breath depends.
devanagari:
न प्राणेन नापानेन मर्त्यो जीवति कश्चन ।

itareṇa tu jīvanti yasminnetāvupāśritau ||
english: No mortal lives by the in-breath or the out-breath. People live by something else, on which these two depend.

school_notes.note: Things that work together, like the parts of a house, serve something other than themselves; so the breaths and senses, working together, depend on a Self that is not a compound, for whose sake they act.
