speaker: Yama
context: Death promises to teach the secret, eternal Brahman, and what happens to the self after death.
devanagari:
हन्त त इदं प्रवक्ष्यामि गुह्यं ब्रह्म सनातनम् ।
यथा च मरणं प्राप्य आत्मा भवति गौतम ॥
iast:
hanta ta idaṃ pravakṣyāmi guhyaṃ brahma sanātanam |
yathā ca maraṇaṃ prāpya ātmā bhavati gautama ||
english: Now, Gautama, I will tell you this secret, eternal Brahman, and what becomes of the self after reaching death.

school_notes.note: Death will teach the hidden, ancient Brahman, by knowing which all worldly existence ends, and, for one who does not know it, how the self goes on after death.

licence: CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wikisource text); underlying Sanskrit work is public domain

speaker: Yama
context: Death says that after death some take new bodies and others become immobile things, according to their deeds and knowledge.
devanagari:
योनिमन्ये प्रपद्यन्ते शरीरत्वाय देहिनः ।
स्थाणुमन्येऽनुसंयन्ति यथाकर्म यथाश्रुतम् ॥
iast:
yonimanye prapadyante śarīratvāya dehinaḥ |
sthāṇumanye'nusaṃyanti yathākarma yathāśrutam ||
english: Some embodied beings enter a womb to take on a body; others pass into a stationary thing, according to their deeds and according to their knowledge.

school_notes.note: The ignorant re-enter a womb to take a body; the lowest become trees and other unmoving things. Each takes a body in keeping with the deeds done and the knowledge gained in this life.

licence: CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wikisource text); underlying Sanskrit work is public domain

speaker: Yama
context: Death identifies the secret Brahman as the person awake in sleepers, shaping desire after desire.
devanagari:
य एष सुप्तेषु जागर्ति कामं कामं पुरुषो निर्मिमाणः ।
तदेव शुक्रं तद्ब्रह्म तदेवामृतमुच्यते ।
तस्मिँल्लोकाः श्रिताः सर्वे तदु नात्येति कश्चन ।
एतद्वै तत् ॥
iast:
ya eṣa supteṣu jāgarti kāmaṃ kāmaṃ puruṣo nirmimāṇaḥ |
tadeva śukraṃ tadbrahma tadevāmṛtamucyate |
tasmim̐llokāḥ śritāḥ sarve tadu nātyeti kaścana |
etadvai tat ||
english: That person who is awake in those who sleep, shaping one desire after another: that is the bright, that is Brahman, that alone is called immortal. In it all the worlds rest, and no one goes beyond it. This, truly, is that.

school_notes.note: When the breath and senses sleep, this Person stays awake, creating the objects of dream through ignorance; that pure one is Brahman, the support of all worlds. Because the teaching of oneness does not stay in minds disturbed by bad logic, scripture repeats it again and again.

licence: CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wikisource text); underlying Sanskrit work is public domain

speaker: Yama
context: Death gives the image of fire: one fire takes the shape of whatever it burns, as the one Self takes every form.
devanagari:
अग्निर्यथैको भुवनं प्रविष्टो
रूपं रूपं प्रतिरूपो बभूव ।
एकस्तथा सर्वभूतान्तरात्मा
रूपं रूपं प्रतिरूपो बहिश्च ॥
iast:
agniryathaiko bhuvanaṃ praviṣṭo
rūpaṃ rūpaṃ pratirūpo babhūva |
ekastathā sarvabhūtāntarātmā
rūpaṃ rūpaṃ pratirūpo bahiśca ||
english: As the one fire, entering the world, takes the form of each thing it meets, so the one Self within all beings takes the form of each, and is also outside.

school_notes.note: As one fire seems many by burning different kinds of wood, the one Self, very subtle, has entered every body and seems to have each form; yet it remains outside, unchanged, like space.

licence: CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wikisource text); underlying Sanskrit work is public domain

speaker: Yama
context: Death repeats the image with the wind: one air takes every shape, as the one Self dwells in all.
devanagari:
वायुर्यथैको भुवनं प्रविष्टो
रूपं रूपं प्रतिरूपो बभूव ।
एकस्तथा सर्वभूतान्तरात्मा
रूपं रूपं प्रतिरूपो बहिश्च ॥
iast:
vāyuryathaiko bhuvanaṃ praviṣṭo
rūpaṃ rūpaṃ pratirūpo babhūva |
ekastathā sarvabhūtāntarātmā
rūpaṃ rūpaṃ pratirūpo bahiśca ||
english: As the one wind, entering the world, takes the form of each thing it meets, so the one Self within all beings takes the form of each, and is also outside.

school_notes.note: The same as before: the wind, entering bodies as breath, takes the form of each; then comes the question whether the one Self must suffer the world's pains.

licence: CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wikisource text); underlying Sanskrit work is public domain

speaker: Yama
context: Death says the one Self in all beings is untouched by the world's suffering, as the sun is untouched by what it shows.
devanagari:
सूर्यो यथा सर्वलोकस्य चक्षुः
न लिप्यते चाक्षुषैर्बाह्यदोषैः ।
एकस्तथा सर्वभूतान्तरात्मा
न लिप्यते लोकदुःखेन बाह्यः ॥
iast:
sūryo yathā sarvalokasya cakṣuḥ
na lipyate cākṣuṣairbāhyadoṣaiḥ |
ekastathā sarvabhūtāntarātmā
na lipyate lokaduḥkhena bāhyaḥ ||
english: As the sun, the eye of the whole world, is not stained by the faults that eyes see, so the one Self within all beings is not stained by the world's suffering, being outside it.

school_notes.note: The sun lights up impure things without being made impure. People suffer through ignorance superimposed on the Self, as a snake is imagined on a rope; the Self, like the rope, is untouched by what is imagined on it.

licence: CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wikisource text); underlying Sanskrit work is public domain

speaker: Yama
context: Death says lasting happiness belongs to those who see the one controller of all within themselves.
devanagari:
एको वशी सर्वभूतान्तरात्मा
एकं रूपं बहुधा यः करोति ।
तमात्मस्थं येऽनुपश्यन्ति धीराः
तेषां सुखं शाश्वतं नेतरेषाम् ॥
iast:
eko vaśī sarvabhūtāntarātmā
ekaṃ rūpaṃ bahudhā yaḥ karoti |
tamātmasthaṃ ye'nupaśyanti dhīrāḥ
teṣāṃ sukhaṃ śāśvataṃ netareṣām ||
english: The one controller, the Self within all beings, who makes his one form many: the wise who see him dwelling within themselves have lasting happiness, and no one else.

school_notes.note: The supreme Lord, with none equal or greater, makes his one pure nature appear many through name and form. Those who turn from outward things and see him within, as a face is seen in a mirror, have the eternal joy of the Self; those attached to outward things do not.

licence: CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wikisource text); underlying Sanskrit work is public domain

speaker: Yama
context: Death says lasting peace belongs to those who see within themselves the eternal among the impermanent.
devanagari:
नित्योऽनित्यानां चेतनश्चेतनानाम्
एको बहूनां यो विदधाति कामान् ।
तमात्मस्थं येऽनुपश्यन्ति धीराः
तेषां शान्तिः शाश्वती नेतरेषाम् ॥
iast:
nityo'nityānāṃ cetanaścetanānām
eko bahūnāṃ yo vidadhāti kāmān |
tamātmasthaṃ ye'nupaśyanti dhīrāḥ
teṣāṃ śāntiḥ śāśvatī netareṣām ||
english: The eternal among the impermanent, the consciousness of all that is conscious, the one who grants the desires of many: the wise who see him dwelling within themselves have lasting peace, and no one else.

school_notes.note: As water burns only through fire, beings are conscious only through the Self's consciousness. The all-knowing Lord effortlessly grants the fruits of their actions to many; those who see him within have eternal peace.

licence: CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wikisource text); underlying Sanskrit work is public domain

speaker: Upanishad
context: The Upanishad voices a seeker's question: how can one know this supreme joy that cannot be described, and does it shine by itself?
devanagari:
तदेतदिति मन्यन्तेऽनिर्देश्यं परमं सुखम् ।
कथं नु तद्विजानीयां किमु भाति विभाति वा ॥
iast:
tadetaditi manyante'nirdeśyaṃ paramaṃ sukham |
kathaṃ nu tadvijānīyāṃ kimu bhāti vibhāti vā ||
english: 'This is that,' they feel: the highest joy, which cannot be described. How can I come to know it? Does it shine by itself, or shine in reflection?

school_notes.note: Renunciants free of desire experience this indescribable joy of self-knowledge as directly present. The seeker asks how they too might know it as 'this', and whether it shines in a way the intellect can grasp; the answer follows: it shines and makes everything shine.

licence: CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wikisource text); underlying Sanskrit work is public domain

speaker: Yama
context: Death answers: Brahman is the light by which sun, moon, stars and fire shine.
devanagari:
न तत्र सूर्यो भाति न चन्द्रतारकं
नेमा विद्युतो भान्ति कुतोऽयमग्निः ।
तमेव भान्तमनुभाति सर्वं
तस्य भासा सर्वमिदं विभाति ॥
iast:
na tatra sūryo bhāti na candratārakaṃ
nemā vidyuto bhānti kuto'yamagniḥ |
tameva bhāntamanubhāti sarvaṃ
tasya bhāsā sarvamidaṃ vibhāti ||
english: There the sun does not shine, nor the moon and stars; these lightnings do not shine, let alone this fire. Everything shines after it as it shines; by its light all this is lit.

school_notes.note: The sun, which reveals everything, does not reveal Brahman, let alone fire. All things shine only after Brahman shines, as a hot coal burns only by the fire in it; so Brahman's own nature is light, for what has no light of its own cannot give light to others.

licence: CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wikisource text); underlying Sanskrit work is public domain

speaker: Yama
context: Death describes the world as an ancient fig tree rooted above, whose root is Brahman (compare Gita 15.1).
devanagari:
ऊर्ध्वमूलोऽवाक्शाख एषोऽश्वत्थः सनातनः ।
तदेव शुक्रं तद्ब्रह्म तदेवामृतमुच्यते ।
तस्मिँल्लोकाः श्रिताः सर्वे तदु नात्येति कश्चन ।
एतद्वै तत् ॥
iast:
ūrdhvamūlo'vākśākha eṣo'śvatthaḥ sanātanaḥ |
tadeva śukraṃ tadbrahma tadevāmṛtamucyate |
tasmim̐llokāḥ śritāḥ sarve tadu nātyeti kaścana |
etadvai tat ||
english: This is the ancient fig tree, with roots above and branches below. That is the bright, that is Brahman, that alone is called immortal. In it all the worlds rest, and no one goes beyond it. This, truly, is that.

school_notes.note: The tree of worldly existence, from the unmanifest down to plants, is called a tree because it is cut down; it is full of birth, ageing, death and grief, changing every moment, hollow like a plantain stem, yet rooted in the highest place of Viṣṇu, Brahman, which is its real essence.

licence: CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wikisource text); underlying Sanskrit work is public domain

speaker: Yama
context: Death says the whole world moves within Brahman, which keeps all in order like a raised thunderbolt.
devanagari:
यदिदं किं च जगत् सर्वं प्राण एजति निःसृतम् ।
महद्भयं वज्रमुद्यतं य एतद्विदुरमृतास्ते भवन्ति ॥
iast:
yadidaṃ kiṃ ca jagat sarvaṃ prāṇa ejati niḥsṛtam |
mahadbhayaṃ vajramudyataṃ ya etadviduramṛtāste bhavanti ||
english: All this world, whatever there is, has come forth from the breath of life and moves in it. It is a great terror, a raised thunderbolt. Those who know this become immortal.

school_notes.note: The 'breath of life' is the supreme Brahman, from which the world comes and in which it moves. Like servants before a master with raised thunderbolt, sun, moon and stars keep their order without pause; knowing this one witness, people become immortal.

licence: CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wikisource text); underlying Sanskrit work is public domain

speaker: Yama
context: Death says the powers of nature keep their order out of awe of Brahman.
devanagari:
भयादस्याग्निस्तपति भयात्तपति सूर्यः ।
भयादिन्द्रश्च वायुश्च मृत्युर्धावति पञ्चमः ॥
iast:
bhayādasyāgnistapati bhayāttapati sūryaḥ |
bhayādindraśca vāyuśca mṛtyurdhāvati pañcamaḥ ||
english: From fear of it fire burns; from fear the sun gives heat; from fear Indra and the Wind, and Death as the fifth, run their course.

school_notes.note: If the powerful guardians of the world had no ruler over them, like a master with a raised thunderbolt, their activity would not be so regular, like that of servants who fear their master.

licence: CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wikisource text); underlying Sanskrit work is public domain

speaker: Yama
context: Death urges knowing Brahman in this life, before the body falls away; otherwise one takes another body.
devanagari:
इह चेदशकद्बोद्धुं प्राक्षरीरस्य विस्रसः ।
ततः सर्गेषु लोकेषु शरीरत्वाय कल्पते ॥
iast:
iha cedaśakadboddhuṃ prākṣarīrasya visrasaḥ |
tataḥ sargeṣu lokeṣu śarīratvāya kalpate ||
english: If one can come to know it here, before the body falls away, [one is freed]; otherwise one becomes fit to take a body again in the created worlds.

school_notes.note: He supplies the missing words: if, while living, one knows Brahman before the body falls, one is freed from bondage; if not, one takes a body in the created worlds. So one should strive for self-knowledge before the body falls.

licence: CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wikisource text); underlying Sanskrit work is public domain

speaker: Yama
context: Death says the Self is seen clearly here, as in a mirror, but only dimly in other worlds.
devanagari:
यथाऽऽदर्शे तथाऽऽत्मनि यथा स्वप्ने तथा पितृलोके ।
यथाऽप्सु परीव ददृशे तथा गन्धर्वलोके
छायातपयोरिव ब्रह्मलोके ॥
iast:
yathā''darśe tathā''tmani yathā svapne tathā pitṛloke |
yathā'psu parīva dadṛśe tathā gandharvaloke
chāyātapayoriva brahmaloke ||
english: As in a mirror, so in oneself; as in a dream, so in the world of the ancestors; as in water, so it appears in the world of the gandharvas; as shade and light, so in the world of Brahman.

school_notes.note: In a clear intellect the Self is seen distinctly, like a face in a mirror; in the world of the ancestors only dimly, as in a dream; in other worlds as a blurred reflection in water; clearly again only in Brahmā's world, which is hard to reach. So one should strive here.

licence: CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wikisource text); underlying Sanskrit work is public domain

speaker: Yama
context: Death says that knowing the senses are separate from the Self, rising and setting on their own, the wise do not grieve.
devanagari:
इन्द्रियाणां पृथग्भावमुदयास्तमयौ च यत् ।
पृथगुत्पद्यमानानां मत्वा धीरो न शोचति ॥
iast:
indriyāṇāṃ pṛthagbhāvamudayāstamayau ca yat |
pṛthagutpadyamānānāṃ matvā dhīro na śocati ||
english: Knowing that the senses are separate, arising separately, and that their rising and setting are their own, the wise do not grieve.

school_notes.note: The senses arise from the elements to grasp their objects and are of a different nature from the pure Self; their rising and setting in waking and sleep belong to them, not to the Self. Knowing this, the wise do not grieve, since the Self never changes; as another scripture says, 'the knower of the Self crosses sorrow'.

licence: CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wikisource text); underlying Sanskrit work is public domain

speaker: Yama
context: Death repeats the inward ladder: senses, mind, intellect, the great self, the unmanifest.
devanagari:
इन्द्रियेभ्यः परं मनो मनसः सत्त्वमुत्तमम् ।
सत्त्वादधि महानात्मा महतोऽव्यक्तमुत्तमम् ॥
iast:
indriyebhyaḥ paraṃ mano manasaḥ sattvamuttamam |
sattvādadhi mahānātmā mahato'vyaktamuttamam ||
english: Beyond the senses is the mind; beyond the mind is the intellect, the highest; beyond the intellect is the great self; beyond the great is the unmanifest, the highest.

school_notes.note: As explained earlier (1.3.10); the objects are included with the senses here, and 'sattva' means the intellect.

licence: CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wikisource text); underlying Sanskrit work is public domain

speaker: Yama
context: Death says beyond the unmanifest is the all-pervading Person; knowing him, one is freed.
devanagari:
अव्यक्तात्तु परः पुरुषो व्यापकोऽलिङ्ग एव च ।
यं ज्ञात्वा मुच्यते जन्तुरमृतत्वं च गच्छति ॥
iast:
avyaktāttu paraḥ puruṣo vyāpako'liṅga eva ca |
yaṃ jñātvā mucyate janturamṛtatvaṃ ca gacchati ||
english: Beyond the unmanifest is the Person, all-pervading and without any mark. Knowing him, a creature is freed and reaches immortality.

school_notes.note: The Person pervades even space, being the cause of all, and has no mark such as the intellect by which it could be inferred. Knowing him through teacher and scripture, one is freed from the knots of ignorance while living, and reaches immortality when the body falls.

licence: CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wikisource text); underlying Sanskrit work is public domain

speaker: Yama
context: Death says the Person cannot be seen with the eye but is grasped by heart and mind.
devanagari:
न संदृशे तिष्ठति रूपमस्य
न चक्षुषा पश्यति कश्चनैनम् ।
हृदा मनीषा मनसाऽभिक्लृप्तो
य एतद्विदुरमृतास्ते भवन्ति ॥
iast:
na saṃdṛśe tiṣṭhati rūpamasya
na cakṣuṣā paśyati kaścanainam |
hṛdā manīṣā manasā'bhiklṛpto
ya etadviduramṛtāste bhavanti ||
english: His form is not within the range of sight; no one sees him with the eye. He is grasped by the heart, by insight, by the mind. Those who know this become immortal.

school_notes.note: No sense can perceive the inner Self; it is revealed to the intellect in the heart, the controller of the mind, through right reflection. Next comes the yoga by which that intellect is gained.

licence: CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wikisource text); underlying Sanskrit work is public domain

speaker: Yama
context: Death describes the highest state of meditation: senses and mind at rest, intellect still.
devanagari:
यदा पञ्चावतिष्ठन्ते ज्ञानानि मनसा सह ।
बुद्धिश्च न विचेष्टते तामाहुः परमां गतिम् ॥
iast:
yadā pañcāvatiṣṭhante jñānāni manasā saha |
buddhiśca na viceṣṭate tāmāhuḥ paramāṃ gatim ||
english: When the five senses come to rest together with the mind, and the intellect does not stir, that, they say, is the highest state.

school_notes.note: When the senses, turned back from their objects, rest in the Self together with the mind, and the deciding intellect does not act, that is called the highest state.

licence: CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wikisource text); underlying Sanskrit work is public domain

speaker: Yama
context: Death defines yoga as the steady holding of the senses and warns that it must be guarded, since it comes and goes.
devanagari:
तां योगमिति मन्यन्ते स्थिरामिन्द्रियधारणाम् ।
अप्रमत्तस्तदा भवति योगो हि प्रभवाप्ययौ ॥
iast:
tāṃ yogamiti manyante sthirāmindriyadhāraṇām |
apramattastadā bhavati yogo hi prabhavāpyayau ||
english: This firm holding of the senses is what they call yoga. Then one must be vigilant, for yoga comes and goes.

school_notes.note: This state is called yoga, though it is really separation from all ills; in it the Self rests in its own nature. Because yoga arises and fades, one must take constant care, being vigilant even before the mind's activity ceases.

licence: CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wikisource text); underlying Sanskrit work is public domain

speaker: Yama
context: Death says the Self cannot be reached by speech, mind or eye; it is grasped only by affirming that it is.
devanagari:
नैव वाचा न मनसा प्राप्तुं शक्यो न चक्षुषा ।
अस्तीति ब्रुवतोऽन्यत्र कथं तदुपलभ्यते ॥
iast:
naiva vācā na manasā prāptuṃ śakyo na cakṣuṣā |
astīti bruvato'nyatra kathaṃ tadupalabhyate ||
english: It cannot be reached by speech, nor by the mind, nor by the eye. How can it be grasped except by one who says, 'It is'?

school_notes.note: Though beyond the senses, the Self exists as the root of the world: when effects are traced back, they end in being, not nothing. One who follows scripture with faith grasps it as 'it is'; one who holds that the world has no root cannot grasp it at all.

licence: CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wikisource text); underlying Sanskrit work is public domain

speaker: Yama
context: Death says the Self is first grasped as existing, and then its true nature becomes clear.
devanagari:
अस्तीत्येवोपलब्धव्यस्तत्त्वभावेन चोभयोः ।
अस्तीत्येवोपलब्धस्य तत्त्वभावः प्रसीदति ॥

astītyevopalabdhavyastattvabhāvena cobhayoḥ |
astītyevopalabdhasya tattvabhāvaḥ prasīdati ||
english: It should be grasped as 'It is', and also in its true nature. For one who has grasped it as 'It is', its true nature becomes clear.

school_notes.note: First the Self is grasped as existing, through its limiting conditions; then its true nature, free of all conditions and beyond 'is' and 'is not', reveals itself to the one who first grasped it as existing.

speaker: Yama
context: Death says that when all the desires lodged in the heart fall away, a mortal becomes immortal here and now.
devanagari:
यदा सर्वे प्रमुच्यन्ते कामा येऽस्य हृदि श्रिताः ।
अथ मर्त्योऽमृतो भवत्यत्र ब्रह्म समश्नुते ॥
iast:
yadā sarve pramucyante kāmā ye'sya hṛdi śritāḥ |
atha martyo'mṛto bhavatyatra brahma samaśnute ||
english: When all the desires that dwell in one's heart are let go, then a mortal becomes immortal and reaches Brahman here.

school_notes.note: Desires rest in the intellect, not the Self; when they fall away, because nothing else remains to be desired, death, which is ignorance, desire and action, is destroyed, and one becomes Brahman right here, like a lamp going out.

speaker: Yama
context: Death says that when all the knots of the heart are cut, a mortal becomes immortal; this is the whole teaching.
devanagari:
यथा सर्वे प्रभिद्यन्ते हृदयस्येह ग्रन्थयः ।
अथ मर्त्योऽमृतो भवत्येतावद्ध्यनुशासनम् ॥
iast:
yathā sarve prabhidyante hṛdayasyeha granthayaḥ |
atha martyo'mṛto bhavatyetāvaddhyanuśāsanam ||
english: When all the knots of the heart are cut here, then a mortal becomes immortal. This much is the teaching.

school_notes.note: The knots are ignorant notions like 'I am this body', 'this wealth is mine', 'I am happy' or 'I am miserable'. When they are cut by knowing 'I am Brahman', the desires they cause perish at the root; this is the whole teaching of the Upanishads, with nothing more to add.

speaker: Yama
context: Death describes the channels of the heart and the path upward through the crown of the head at death.
devanagari:
शतं चैका च हृदयस्य नाड्य-
स्तासां मूर्धानमभिनिःसृतैका ।
तयोर्ध्वमायन्नमृतत्वमेति
विष्वङ्ङन्या उत्क्रमणे भवन्ति ॥
iast:
śataṃ caikā ca hṛdayasya nāḍya-
stāsāṃ mūrdhānamabhiniḥsṛtaikā |
tayordhvamāyannamṛtatvameti
viṣvaṅṅanyā utkramaṇe bhavanti ||
english: A hundred and one are the channels of the heart; one of them goes up to the crown of the head. Going up by it, one reaches immortality; the others lead in every direction at the time of departure.

school_notes.note: One channel, suṣumnā, passes through the crown; directing the self into it at death, one goes up through the sun to a relative immortality, or reaches full immortality with Brahmā later. The other channels lead back into worldly life. This concerns those who know Brahman only partly, since the full knower goes nowhere.

speaker: Yama
context: Death sums up the teaching: draw out the inner Self from the body as a reed's stalk is drawn from its sheath.
devanagari:
अङ्गुष्ठमात्रः पुरुषोऽन्तरात्मा
सदा जनानां हृदये संनिविष्टः ।
तं स्वाच्छरीरात्प्रवृहेन्मुञ्जादिवेषीकां धैर्येण ।
तं विद्याच्छुक्रममृतं तं विद्याच्छुक्रममृतमिति ॥
iast:
aṅguṣṭhamātraḥ puruṣo'ntarātmā
sadā janānāṃ hṛdaye saṃniviṣṭaḥ |
taṃ svāccharīrātpravṛhenmuñjādiveṣīkāṃ dhairyeṇa |
taṃ vidyācchukramamṛtaṃ taṃ vidyācchukramamṛtamiti ||
english: The Person the size of a thumb, the inner Self, always dwells in the heart of people. One should draw him out from one's own body with steadiness, as the stalk is drawn from a reed. One should know him as the bright, the immortal; one should know him as the bright, the immortal.

school_notes.note: 'Draw out' means separate in understanding: distinguish the Self from the body with steady care, as the inner stalk is pulled from a reed, and know that pure consciousness as the immortal Brahman. The repetition marks the end of the Upanishad.

speaker: Upanishad
context: The Upanishad concludes the story: Nachiketas, taught by Death, reached Brahman, and so can anyone who knows the Self.
devanagari:
मृत्युप्रोक्तां नचिकेतोऽथ लब्ध्वा
विद्यामेतां योगविधिं च कृत्स्नम् ।
ब्रह्मप्राप्तो विरजोऽभूद्विमृत्यु-
रन्योऽप्येवं यो विदध्यात्ममेव ॥
iast:
mṛtyuproktāṃ naciketo'tha labdhvā
vidyāmetāṃ yogavidhiṃ ca kṛtsnam |
brahmaprāpto virajo'bhūdvimṛtyu-
ranyo'pyevaṃ yo vidadhyātmameva ||
english: Having received this knowledge taught by Death, and the whole practice of yoga, Nachiketas reached Brahman, free of stain and free of death; and so will anyone else who knows the inner Self in this way.

school_notes.note: This conclusion of the story praises the knowledge. Nachiketas, freed from merit and demerit, desire and ignorance, reached Brahman; anyone else who knows the inner Self as Nachiketas did becomes the same.

speaker: teacher and student
context: The Upanishad closes with the traditional peace chant for teacher and student, asking that they never turn against each other.
devanagari:
सह नाववतु ।
सह नौ भुनक्तु ।
सह वीर्यं करवावहै ।
तेजस्विनावधीतमस्तु मा विद्विषावहै ॥
iast:
saha nāvavatu |
saha nau bhunaktu |
saha vīryaṃ karavāvahai |
tejasvināvadhītamastu mā vidviṣāvahai ||
english: May he protect us both together. May he nourish us both together. May we work together with vigour. May our study be full of light. May we not hate each other.

school_notes.note: This peace chant removes faults arising from careless teaching or study. May the Lord revealed by the Upanishad protect us by revealing knowledge and nourish us with its fruit; may teacher and student never bear ill will towards each other through faults in teaching or learning; 'peace' is said three times to quiet every fault.
